title: Arithmetic types, completions and certified p-adic precision
central_question: Which arithmetic statements survive a change of scalar domain, and what can a finite p-adic calculation actually certify?
synopsis: An arithmetic expression includes its scalar ring, topology and precision. The rational field, a p-adic completion, a residue ring and a formal power-series ring support different operations. A unital homomorphism between characteristic zero and characteristic p would send the nonzero integer p both to an invertible element and to zero, an immediate obstruction when the source is a field. Completion instead preserves rational identities while changing which sequences converge. These distinctions turn the early request to separate meanings of Q into a practical specification for every later lifting algorithm. The useful output is a compatible sequence of exact congruences accompanied by derivative and residual valuations. Such a sequence proves an existence statement only with a convergence argument; a zero residue at one precision cannot certify an exact zero. Perfectoid and prismatic language extends this discipline, but carries additional structural hypotheses rather than merely renaming small errors.

A precision-N representative specifies a coset modulo p^N.","For a nonzero integral series F=Σa_nT^n, μ(F)=min v_p(a_n), and λ(F) is the first index attaining that minimum. Infinite tails must be controlled before certifying these minima."]
theorem_statement: If f∈Z_p[X] and a_n is a root modulo p^n with unit derivative, there is exactly one a_(n+1)=a_n+t p^n modulo p^(n+1) reducing to a_n. The compatible sequence converges to the unique root of f in a_1+pZ_p.
theorem_proof: Taylor expansion modulo p^(n+1) gives f(a_n+t p^n)≡f(a_n)+t p^n f′(a_n), since all terms of order two are divisible by p^(2n). Dividing by p^n gives one linear equation for t modulo p. The derivative is a unit, so t is unique. Successive representatives differ by an element of p^nZ_p and hence form a Cauchy sequence. Completeness supplies a limit a; continuity of polynomial evaluation gives f(a)=0. If b is a second root in the same residue class, factor f(a)−f(b)=(a−b)g(a,b). The reduction of g is the nonzero derivative at a_1, so g is a unit and a=b. Newton's update a−f(a)/f′(a) accelerates the same argument: an initial residual valuation at least n becomes at least 2n when the derivative is a unit. An exact vanishing claim requires this theorem or a separate identity, whereas finite arithmetic alone establishes only congruences.

title: Divisor incidence, valuations and constructive integer parametrization
central_question: How can multiplicative arithmetic become a finite lattice calculation with a complete certificate?
synopsis: Prime factorization converts multiplication into addition of exponent vectors. Divisibility becomes a coordinate order, gcd and lcm become coordinate minimum and maximum, and a monomial equation becomes an integer linear system at every prime. This does more than simplify computation: it states exactly which sign cases, valuation bounds and prime supports a complete answer must cover. Divisor incidence then transports scalar arithmetic identities into matrix factorizations. The same identity n=Σ_(d|n)φ(d) controls a positive gcd kernel, its determinant, and a sieve implementation. Thus arithmetic, combinatorics and finite-dimensional energy geometry meet through a declared transform, not merely because they share the word prime. The family includes factorial valuations and prime-stripped block products: one computes the p-power removed, the other computes the remaining unit, and their recombination reconstructs the original factorial exactly.
definitions_json: ["For n=∏p_i^a_i, a divisor corresponds to exponents 0≤b_i≤a_i. Its divisor lattice is the product of chains C_(a_i+1).","Dirichlet convolution is (f*g)(n)=Σ_(d|n)f(d)g(n/d). The incidence matrix E has E_(i,d)=1 when d divides i, and zero otherwise.","Legendre’s formula gives v_p(n!)=Σ_(j≥1)⌊n/p^j⌋. The stripped unit U_p(n)=n!/p^v_p(n!) is an integer not divisible by p."]
theorem_statement: For G_(i,j)=gcd(i,j), 1≤i,j≤N, one has G=E diag(φ(1),…,φ(N))Eᵀ. Consequently G is positive definite and det G=∏_(d=1)^Nφ(d). Moreover positive solutions of x²y³=2²⁰3¹² are exactly x=2^(10−3r)3^(6−3s), y=2^(2r)3^(2s), with 0≤r≤3 and 0≤s≤2.
theorem_proof: The (i,j) entry of the displayed matrix product is Σ_(d|i,d|j)φ(d)=Σ_(d|gcd(i,j))φ(d)=gcd(i,j). The identity Σ_(d|m)φ(d)=m follows by grouping 1,…,m according to gcd with m. E is lower triangular with diagonal one; every φ(d)>0, giving positive definiteness and the determinant. For the monomial equation, a prime outside {2,3} has 2v_p(x)+3v_p(y)=0, forcing both exponents zero. At p=2, nonnegative integral solutions to 2a+3b=20 require b=2r and a=10−3r, with r=0,1,2,3. At p=3 the same argument gives b=2s and a=6−3s, with s=0,1,2. Independent choices prove both existence and completeness of the twelve solutions. A bounded search would show existence of examples but would not establish that no extra prime or exponent pattern occurs.

title: Cyclotomic degrees, Galois fibres and trace transport
central_question: What exact structure follows from conductor 1680, and which additional certificates are needed to connect it to another representation?
synopsis: The number 384 becomes mathematically productive when assigned a specific role: it is the degree of Q(ζ₁₆₈₀), not the order of a primitive root, the largest Galois-element order, a Lie algebra dimension or a category rank. Distinguishing those meanings allows a much stronger construction. The subgroup corresponding to Q(ζ₃₀) produces uniform fibres of size 48; trace transport is then a theorem of the field tower and can be checked through finite residue classes. This organizes a recurring numerical framework into an auditable arithmetic object. The same discipline applies to trace orthogonality: a coefficient p, rather than p+1, follows from which residue sums are actually being taken. Any proposed passage to an integral E₈ lattice must exhibit a basis matrix, its Gram form and an intertwining equation. Equal degree or a handful of coincident traces cannot supply those maps.

Relative trace is a linear map, not a choice of an integral basis."]
theorem_statement: Let K=Q(ζ₁₆₈₀), L=Q(ζ₃₀), and η=ζ₁₆₈₀^56. Then [K:Q]=384, [L:Q]=8, [K:L]=48; reduction U₁₆₈₀→U₃₀ is onto with every fibre of size 48. Hence Tr_(K/Q)(η^n)=48c₃₀(n). The Galois group of K is C₄²×C₂³×C₃ and has exponent 12.
theorem_proof: Since 1680=16·3·5·7, the totient product is 8·2·4·6=384; φ(30)=1·2·4=8. The order of ζ₁₆₈₀^56 is 1680/gcd(1680,56)=30, giving L⊆K and the tower degree. A class coprime to 30 can be extended to a unit modulo 1680 by prescribing a compatible odd residue modulo 16 and a nonzero residue modulo 7; CRT proves surjectivity. A surjective finite-group homomorphism has fibres equal to kernel cosets, all of size 384/8. Summing η^(an) across these fibres proves the trace formula. For the group structure CRT gives U₁₆×U₃×U₅×U₇≅(C₄×C₂)×C₂×C₄×C₆, and C₆≅C₂×C₃. The least common multiple of these cyclic orders is 12, so the group cannot be cyclic of order 384. These conclusions use classical cyclotomic irreducibility as a structural input; the residue enumeration independently verifies the finite arithmetic.

title: Quadratic units, complete Pell orbits and congruence populations
central_question: When does a recurrence describe every integer solution, and how do finite congruence filters change an infinite population?
synopsis: A norm-preserving recurrence generates solutions immediately; proving that it generates all of them is the substantive step. The D=2 Pell equation has an elementary descent to the identity, while the negative equation x²−2y²=−7 requires two distinct canonical seeds. A compact reduction interval makes the seed count finite and proves uniqueness. This exposes an important difference between a finite list, an infinite parametrized family, and a complete classification. Once completeness is established, modular arithmetic is useful again: the unit recurrence is invertible modulo every q, so its state orbit is genuinely periodic. Counting accepted index classes gives an exact density within the orbit and a logarithmic coefficient in a height-bounded population. The same quadratic-unit mechanism explains Fibonacci matrix eigenvalues, but geometric length normalizations must still be declared separately.
definitions_json: ["In Z[√2], conjugation sends x+y√2 to x−y√2 and the norm is x²−2y². The norm-one unit ε=3+2√2 has inverse 3−2√2.","Multiplication by ε sends (x,y) to (3x+4y,2x+3y), an integral matrix of determinant one.","A canonical seed is a norm solution reduced to a specified half-open interval under multiplication by ε. A modular filter is a predicate on the full residue state, not solely on a visually selected coordinate."]
theorem_statement: Every solution x,y≥0 of x²−2y²=1 is ε^j for a unique j≥0. Every solution of x²−2y²=−7 with y>0 belongs uniquely to (1+2√2)ε^j or (5+4√2)ε^j, j∈Z. For the positive Pell orbit, a modulo-q predicate accepting w positions in its period P yields a population (w/P)log N/log ε+O(1) under y≤N.
theorem_proof: For norm one and y>0, y≥2 and √2<x/y≤3/2. The inverse step gives x′=3x−4y>0 and 0≤y′=3y−2x<y; iteration reaches (1,0), proving coverage. For norm −7, α=x+y√2 is positive whenever y>0. Multiply by a unique power of ε to put β in [√7,ε√7). Since β̄=−7/β, its coordinates satisfy x_β=(β−7/β)/2≥0 and y_β=(β+7/β)/(2√2), which lies below 3√(7/2)<6. Thus y_β∈{2,3,4,5}; the required squares 2y_β²−7 are 1,11,25,43. Exactly two seeds remain. The interval is half-open, so seed and exponent are unique. For the positive orbit, conjugation gives y_j=(ε^j−ε^(−j))/(2√2), hence j≤log N/log ε+O(1). The determinant-one recurrence permutes a finite modular state set, so its orbit has no transient tail. A periodic acceptance pattern with w of P positions contributes w/P of the indices, up to a bounded endpoint error.

title: Number fields, norm forms and arithmetic obstructions
central_question: Which field, ideal and lattice data are sufficient to turn a norm identity into a complete arithmetic statement?
synopsis: A defining polynomial is the beginning of a number-field calculation. Irreducibility, the polynomial-order index, ramification, unit structure and the actual sublattice representing the original equation each impose additional requirements. The squarefree discriminants −23 and −283 give unusually clean maximal-order certificates, while nonabelian Galois closure supplies a decisive obstruction to cyclotomic containment. The class-field examples add a second kind of obstruction: an extension with the right degree can still ramify at finite or real places. Finally, the 2026 norm forms show why unit transport alone need not classify a two-variable equation. Multiplication preserves a cubic norm surface, but often leaves the binary plane that encoded the original problem. Retaining the embedding lattice makes this loss visible and turns a plausible reduction into a mathematically correct one.
definitions_json: ["For an algebraic integer α, the discriminant of Z[α] equals the field discriminant times [O_K:Z[α]]². A squarefree polynomial discriminant therefore forces index one.","The field norm N_(K/Q)(x) is the determinant of multiplication by x on K. In a specified integral order, norm ±1 implies a unit of that order.","A binary cubic equation can embed in a norm equation only together with a rank-two lattice condition; the full norm surface has an extra coordinate. An exceptional unit is an algebraic integer z for which both z and 1−z are units."]
theorem_statement: For f(T)=T³−T+1, irreducibility and discriminant −23 imply S₃ Galois closure and exclude every root from every cyclotomic field. Separately, in the order Z[z] with z³=−4, N(a+bz+cz²)=a³−4b³+16c³+12abc; norm-one transport need not preserve c=0.
theorem_proof: The only possible rational roots of the monic cubic are ±1, neither of which is a root. Its discriminant is −4(−1)³−27=−23, not a rational square. An irreducible cubic has transitive Galois group A₃ or S₃; the discriminant-square criterion excludes A₃. Every subfield of a finite abelian Galois extension is itself Galois because every subgroup is normal. A nonnormal cubic with S₃ closure therefore cannot be contained in a cyclotomic field. For the norm formula, multiplication by a+bz+cz² in basis (1,z,z²) has matrix [[a,−4c,−4b],[b,a,−4c],[c,b,a]]. Its determinant is the displayed form, giving an exact integral certificate without approximate roots. The unit ε=1−z−z² has norm one. Multiplying the binary element −1−3z by ε gives −13−2z+4z². Both have norm 107, but the latter has nonzero third coordinate. Consequently unit-orbit completeness in the ambient order, even if independently proved, would still require an exact return-to-plane test to solve u³+4v³=107.

title: Modular forms, Hecke relations and arithmetic local factors
central_question: Which identities genuinely characterize modular arithmetic, rather than an arbitrary prime-indexed statistic?
synopsis: A modular-form assertion includes the group, weight, character, normalization and transformation law. Once those are fixed, dimensions, Hecke recurrences and Euler factors become exact algebraic constraints. The number 24 enters the logarithmic derivative of Dedekind eta through a specific product normalization; it is not interchangeable with a root count or an abstract dimension. Similarly, a genuine Frobenius trace is tied to a point count and determinant p. Its symmetric square has three eigenvalue products, not a guessed two-factor denominator. This family places q-expansion calculations beside local arithmetic while retaining the distinction between an Eisenstein series, a cusp eigenform and an elliptic-curve L-function. Modular symbols supply a boundary algebra that can later support periods, but their elementary relations alone do not execute a modular-symbol algorithm or establish modularity.

The symmetric square eigenvalues are α²,p,β²."]
theorem_statement: The weight-38 full-level modular-form space has basis E₄⁸E₆, E₄⁵E₆³, E₄²E₆⁵ and dimension three; its cusp subspace is ΔM₂₆ of dimension two. For elliptic eigenvalues α,β, the symmetric-square denominator is 1−(a_p²−p)t+p(a_p²−p)t²−p³t³.
theorem_proof: A monomial E₄^aE₆^b has weight 4a+6b. Solving 4a+6b=38 in nonnegative integers gives b=1,3,5 and a=8,5,2. Polynomial independence in C[E₄,E₆] proves that these monomials form a basis. Multiplication by the nonzero Δ identifies cusp forms of weight 38 with weight-26 forms, whose equation 4a+6b=26 has solutions (a,b)=(5,1),(2,3). The structural description of the modular-form ring and its cusp ideal are classical inputs, while the dimension calculation is elementary. For the symmetric square, α²+β²=(α+β)²−2αβ=a_p²−2p. Adding the middle eigenvalue p gives sum a_p²−p. The sum of pairwise products is p(α²+β²)+p²=p(a_p²−p), and the triple product is p³. Expanding the three linear factors gives the stated polynomial. The determinant p is essential: substituting an unrelated prime-power ratio destroys this derivation.

title: Euler products, prime sums and the analytic burden of identification
central_question: How do multiplicative identities become analytic formulas without losing signs, prime powers, convergence or main terms?
synopsis: The divisor algebra gives formal identities; absolute convergence permits their interpretation as analytic functions. This transition is where several recovered proposals needed repair. Pointwise μΛ is a negative prime indicator weighted by logarithm, while convolution μ*log equals the positive prime-power function Λ. A prime-ideal sum changes again when norms and splitting types enter. An Euler product in Re(s)>1 is nonvanishing there, but this fact does not settle zeros after analytic continuation. Likewise π(x) and x/log x are not interchangeable at square-root error scale: the omitted x/log²x term is much larger. The family organizes these issues around exact operation and domain. Spectral determinants, sampled zeta layouts and prime oscillatory tones can be valid mathematical objects while their proposed identification with arithmetic zeros remains an additional, explicitly missing theorem.

The Möbius function μ vanishes on integers with a squared prime factor.","A Dirichlet series is absolutely convergent where Σ|a_n|n^(−σ) is finite; only in a justified domain may one freely multiply, rearrange or differentiate the relevant series.","The arithmetic prime sums θ(x)=Σ_(p≤x)log p and ψ(x)=Σ_(p^k≤x)log p differ by prime-power contributions. A spectral zeta requires its own operator, eigenvalue domain and summability."]
theorem_statement: The exact convolution identity μ*log=Λ gives −ζ′(s)/ζ(s)=ΣΛ(n)n^(−s) for Re(s)>1. Also Σφ(n)n^(−s)=ζ(s−1)/ζ(s) for Re(s)>2, and for real σ>2 its tail after N is at most N^(2−σ)/(σ−2).
theorem_proof: For n=∏p_i^a_i, log n=Σ_(d|n)Λ(d), since the prime powers dividing n contribute Σ_i a_i log p_i. Convolution with μ, using μ*1=ε, gives μ*log=Λ. Absolute convergence in σ>1 justifies differentiating the Euler product and summing its geometric prime-power expansions. By contrast μ(n)Λ(n) is −log p at n=p and zero elsewhere, because μ(p^k)=0 for k≥2; its sum is −θ(x), not ψ(x). For the totient identity, n=Σ_(d|n)φ(d) means id=1*φ. Multiplication of absolutely convergent Dirichlet series in σ>2 gives ζ(s−1)=ζ(s)Σφ(n)n^(−s); the Euler product ensures ζ(s)≠0 there. Since 0≤φ(n)≤n, the remaining tail is bounded by Σ_(n>N)n^(1−σ)≤∫_N^∞x^(1−σ)dx. This explicitly states both the stronger half-plane required by φ(n) and an error certificate for truncation.

title: Algebraic maps, singularities and the choice of smooth model
central_question: Which geometric information is preserved by a parametrization, a birational coordinate change or a normalization?
synopsis: An equation is not yet a complete specification of the geometric object being studied. An affine curve may be singular, its normalization smooth, and its projective closure may acquire additional points at infinity. A parametrization can be injective and still lose differential information. Conversely, an explicit rational change of coordinate can identify function fields even when the displayed equations look unrelated. This family builds a hierarchy of certificates: substitution proves that a map lands on the curve; an inverse on a dense open proves birationality; an integral-closure argument proves normalization; Jacobian or local-ring calculations detect singularities; ramification on the smooth compact model determines genus. Cross-ratio symmetry supplies a finite quotient of ordered configurations, but singular special values and ramification must be handled before treating a parameter as a moduli coordinate.
definitions_json: ["A normalization replaces an integral curve by the curve whose coordinate ring is integrally closed in its function field. A birational map is an isomorphism of function fields, not necessarily an everywhere-defined isomorphism.","For a plane curve F=0 in characteristic zero, a point with F=F_x=F_y=0 is singular. Local intersection multiplicity measures the length of the corresponding local quotient when finite.","For squarefree P of degree m and d≥2, the superelliptic curve means the smooth projective normalization of y^d=P(x), with δ=gcd(d,m) points over infinity."]
theorem_statement: The cusp y²=x³ is normalized by t↦(t²,t³), and its intersection multiplicity with y=0 at the origin is three. For squarefree P of degree m, the smooth projective model of y^d=P(x) has genus g=((d−1)(m−1)−gcd(d,m)+1)/2.
theorem_proof: The ring A=C[t²,t³] has fraction field C(t), since t=t³/t², and t is integral over A because it satisfies T²−t²=0. C[t] is integrally closed and finite over A, so it is the normalization. The cusp is singular at the origin because the two partial derivatives of y²−x³ vanish there; the parametrization derivative is also zero there, explaining why injectivity does not imply an immersion. Quotienting the local equation by y gives C[x]_(x)/(x³), whose length is three. In the blowup chart y=ux, the total equation is x²(u²−x)=0 and the strict transform u²−x=0 is smooth. For the superelliptic genus, each of the m simple finite zeros has ramification index d, contributing d−1. At infinity there are δ points, each of index d/δ, contributing d−δ in total. Riemann–Hurwitz gives 2g−2=−2d+m(d−1)+(d−δ). Rearrangement yields the stated formula. Both the squarefree assumption and the use of the smooth compact normalization are essential.

title: Elliptic arithmetic: local counts, global points and height lattices
central_question: How far can exact local and group-law certificates take us toward rational rank, and where do descent and global conjectures enter?
synopsis: Elliptic arithmetic joins several structures whose numerical outputs must not be conflated. A point count over a finite field gives a Frobenius trace. A rational group-law calculation gives an exact point and its multiples. Good reduction can rule out rational torsion, producing a rank lower bound from one nonzero point. A height pairing then certifies independence and measures the covolume of a chosen subgroup, while a Selmer computation can give an upper bound with an additional Tate–Shafarevich contribution. Each is valuable on its own. The most coherent cross-year example is E:y²+y=x³−x, of discriminant 37: exact finite counts in 2024 recur as group and rank certificates in 2026. That continuity supports a reusable arithmetic laboratory recipe, while the stronger assertions of exact rank, BSD or complete integral points need separate proofs.
definitions_json: ["For a good prime p, a_p=p+1−#E(F_p) and the local polynomial is 1−a_p t+pt². Good reduction means the discriminant is nonzero modulo p.","For E:y²+y=x³−x, negation is (x,y)↦(x,−y−1). Rational points form an abelian group with identity O.","The canonical height pairing is positive definite on E(Q) modulo torsion. A Gram determinant for a subgroup of index I is I² times the full-lattice regulator."]
theorem_statement: For E:y²+y=x³−x, the rational torsion subgroup is trivial and P=(0,0) has infinite order, so rank E(Q)≥1. The exact point counts #E(F₅)=8 and #E(F₇)=9 suffice, provided the prime-to-p restriction on torsion reduction is respected.
theorem_proof: The discriminant is 37, so both primes are good. Suppose there is a rational torsion point of prime order ℓ. If ℓ≠5, injection of ℓ-torsion under reduction at 5 forces ℓ|8 and thus ℓ=2. Reduction at 7 then forces 2|9, impossible. If ℓ=5, reduction at 7 instead forces 5|9, also impossible. Every nontrivial finite abelian torsion group contains an element of prime order, so all rational torsion is excluded. The point (0,0) is nonzero and lies on E, hence has infinite order. This proves a rank lower bound without computing an L-function. For heights, bilinearity gives G′=MᵀGM under a generator-coordinate matrix M and therefore det G′=(det M)²det G. A positive Gram determinant proves independence of the displayed points but says nothing about saturation unless the index is certified. The exact Selmer sequence adds the separate quotient Sha[n] to E(Q)/nE(Q); a Selmer cardinality is therefore not automatically a count of visible rational generators.

Exact addition gives 7P=(−5/9,8/27), where both sides of the equation are 280/729. title: Divisors, compactification and projective positivity
central_question: What separate certificates establish a smooth quotient, a well-behaved boundary, positivity and an actual projective embedding?
synopsis: The early arithmetic-geometry material becomes coherent when organized around distinct geometric properties. Neatness removes finite stabilizer phenomena in an open arithmetic quotient. A compactification adds boundary strata. Regular cones make local toric charts smooth. A positive canonical or log-canonical divisor controls a birational growth property. A sufficiently positive line bundle supplies sections that define an embedding. None of these steps is interchangeable with the others. Modular curves make this hierarchy unusually explicit: X(3) is a smooth genus-zero compact curve, while its four-punctured interior is hyperbolic and of log-general type. Divisor intersection on P¹×P¹ then gives a second exact arena for positivity and invariant classes. The family’s strongest result is a curve embedding criterion whose proof states exactly why enough sections separate both points and tangent directions.

On a smooth curve, separation of every length-two subscheme is the relevant section criterion.","A two-dimensional toric cone with primitive generators u,v is regular when |det(u,v)|=1. Smoothness is local lattice regularity; projectivity additionally requires a compatible support function."]
theorem_statement: For a smooth projective curve of genus g and a line bundle L of degree d≥2g+1, h⁰(L)=d+1−g and the complete linear system embeds X into P^(d−g). On the principal modular curve X(3), deg K=−2 while deg(K+D)=2; at level seven these degrees are four and 28.
theorem_proof: For any length-two subscheme Z, Serre duality gives H¹(L(−Z)) dual to H⁰(K_X⊗L⁻¹(Z)). Its degree is 2g−2−d+2≤−1, so it has no nonzero section. The restriction sequence therefore makes H⁰(L)→H⁰(L|_Z) surjective. Distinct points and doubled points give point separation and tangent separation; the length-one version also gives base-point freeness. The standard embedding criterion then proves very ampleness. Vanishing of H¹(L), followed by Riemann–Roch, yields h⁰(L)=d+1−g. For a torsion-free effective modular group of index μ and c cusps, Gauss–Bonnet gives 2g−2+c=μ/6. Principal level N has c=μ/N. At N=3, μ=12,c=4,g=0; at N=7, μ=168,c=24,g=3. The degree formulas then distinguish ordinary from logarithmic general type. These arguments use the declared smooth projective curve and classical modular-curve inputs; they do not algebraize an arbitrary analytic space.

title: Cohomological realizations, Hodge filtrations and comparison types
central_question: Which information survives a realization, and what additional structure is required before two cohomology theories can be compared?
synopsis: Cohomology provides several forms of organized information: dimensions, graded pieces, mixed structures, integral torsion, Frobenius action and functorial maps. A numerical realization may preserve addition and multiplication while forgetting almost everything else. This is why an Euler characteristic can be zero for a nontrivial elliptic curve, and why multiplying it by Shannon entropy cannot automatically become a positive complexity index. The same caution governs comparison theorems: a characteristic-p variety has no complex analytic space until appropriate characteristic-zero data have been supplied, and a motivic chain index is not a singular cohomology degree. A finite monodromy model makes the loss of information especially concrete. Rational ranks can remain unchanged while integer coinvariants gain torsion; the nilpotent operator determines a weight filtration but not an entire limiting mixed Hodge structure.

A motivic realization is a declared ring homomorphism out of that ring.","Compact-support Euler characteristic is χ_c(X)=Σ_i(−1)^i dim H_c^i(X); it is additive but need not be positive or separating.","A monodromy weight filtration centered at one obeys N(W_k)⊆W_(k−2) and N^j:Gr_(1+j)^W→Gr_(1−j)^W isomorphically. A Hodge filtration and polarization are extra data."]
theorem_statement: For V=Qe₁⊕Qe₂ and N(e₂)=e₁,N(e₁)=0, the centered weight filtration is W_k=0 for k<0, W₀=W₁=Qe₁ and W_k=V for k≥2. For integral monodromy M_n=I+nN, n>0, the coinvariants are Z⊕Z/nZ, although all these rational models have the same ranks.
theorem_proof: The image and kernel of N are both Qe₁. The proposed filtration lowers by two under N, and its only nonzero graded pieces are Gr₀ and Gr₂, both one-dimensional. N maps the class of e₂ to the class of e₁, an isomorphism, while all higher required isomorphisms concern zero spaces. Thus the defining conditions are satisfied. On the integer lattice, (M_n−I)Z²=nZe₁, so the quotient is generated freely by e₂ and by e₁ modulo n. Tensoring with Q removes the latter torsion. For realization loss, the scissor relation A¹={0}⊔G_m gives [G_m]=L−1. Compact-support cohomology of G_m has one copy of the coefficient field in degrees one and two, so its Euler characteristic is zero despite nonzero cohomology. A projective genus-g curve has Betti numbers (1,2g,1) and Euler characteristic 2−2g. Therefore χ_c(X)H(p) can vanish or be negative for a positive entropy H(p). Additivity alone gives no positivity or faithful geometric encoding.

title: Typed operations, quotients and finite algebraic structure
central_question: Which operations, equations and equivalences actually determine an algebra, and which information survives quotienting?
synopsis:
The algebraic backbone of the collection is the move from a named collection of symbols to a multiplication law whose identities can be proved. A field, a monoid, a ring and a partial resource algebra have different admissible operations. Their quotients therefore require different compatibility conditions. The useful revised question is not whether a construction looks algebraic, but whether its carrier, operations, units, domains of definition and notion of equality have all been specified. This viewpoint makes the number-system comparisons, transported operations, finite maximal ideals, capped trace monoids and squarefree branch decomposition parts of one coherent programme.

Transport of structure is the first constructive tool. Given a bijection, pulling all operations back creates an isomorphic object, so associativity and distributivity are inherited by proof. This gives a complete model of a coordinate deformation while explaining why it supplies no new intrinsic field invariant. Quotients then remove information in a controlled way: a ring congruence is determined by a two-sided ideal; a monoid quotient requires a multiplication-compatible equivalence; a partial algebra needs its composability relation retained. Approximate numerical closeness cannot silently serve as any of these equalities.

Finite models make the distinction executable. Enumerating ideals of a finite ring can produce maximal ideals and field quotients. Capping an additive counter produces an absorbing top layer, but does not turn its semigroup kernel into a linear nullspace. The latter distinction matters throughout the atlas: a minimal two-sided ideal, a kernel of a homomorphism and a vector-space kernel answer different questions. Algebra becomes useful for interactive reconstruction precisely when the requested invariant is named before its computation.
definitions_json: ["For a unital ring R, a quotient R/I is defined by a two-sided ideal I; multiplication of classes is [a][b]=[ab].","For a finite monoid S, K(S) denotes its unique minimal nonempty two-sided ideal. It is not a matrix nullspace.","For k≥1, L_k={0,…,k} has operation a⊕b=min(a+b,k); k is absorbing.","For a bijection φ:X→Y, transported multiplication is x⋆y=φ⁻¹(φ(x)φ(y)), with all other required operations transported likewise."]
theorem_statement: For a finite monoid S and positive integers k_1,…,k_r, K(S×∏L_{k_i})=K(S)×{(k_1,…,k_r)}. Thus adding saturated counters preserves the cardinality of the minimal ideal, although it enlarges the monoid.
theorem_proof: Let P=S×∏L_{k_i}. The displayed product J is a nonempty two-sided ideal: multiplication preserves K(S), while every capped coordinate remains at its maximum. Let I be any nonempty two-sided ideal of P and choose (s,a)∈I. Multiplication by (1,k_1,…,k_r) puts (s,k_1,…,k_r) in I. The set of x∈S for which (x,k_1,…,k_r)∈I is a nonempty ideal of S. It contains K(S), hence I contains J. Therefore J is the unique minimal ideal. For completeness, existence and uniqueness of K(S) in a finite monoid follow by choosing a minimal nonempty ideal and observing that the product of any two nonempty ideals is nonempty and lies in their intersection. Minimality then forces the two chosen minimal ideals to agree. This proof concerns multiplication ideals only; no vector-space structure is used.

title: Exact matrix structure, metrics and spectral certificates
central_question: Which finite identities certify rank, spectrum and decomposition, and which metric is each certificate using?
synopsis:
Linear algebra is a common language across the source years, but a useful synthesis must preserve the question encoded by each matrix. Rank counts independent directions, singular values quantify amplification after metrics are fixed, Jordan structure measures nilpotent mixing, and a projector certifies a subspace only through its defining identities. A large Frobenius norm, a symmetry label and an eigenvalue list cannot replace one another. The revised framework starts with a domain, codomain and scalar field, then attaches the appropriate certificate.

The exact approach is particularly effective when a numerical claim can be reduced to polynomial identities. A verified factorization A=UV supplies a rank upper bound; a nonzero minor supplies a lower bound. Reduction modulo a prime can certify that a rational minor is nonzero, while a rank drop modulo that prime can arise from arithmetic cancellation. A spectral polynomial p(T)=0 gives projectors only when its roots are distinct; actual nonzero support witnesses are still needed to certify that every advertised eigenvalue occurs. These are constructive, inspectable statements rather than a generic reliance on diagonalization software.

Metrics are part of this structure. A diagonalizable matrix with real spectrum can be self-adjoint in a suitable positive metric without being symmetric in the original coordinates. Conversely a nontrivial Jordan block cannot be made self-adjoint by a positive metric, because an isometric change to ordinary Euclidean coordinates would make it diagonalizable. The same rule governs anisotropy and whitening: coordinate changes preserve metric singular values only when both source and target metrics transform. This family supplies algebraic certificates which the inverse, control and statistical chapters can then use with their own observation and error models.
definitions_json: ["A rank certificate pairs an exact rank-r factorization with a nonzero r×r minor.","A positive metric η defines ⟨x,y⟩_η=x*ηy; η-self-adjointness is A*η=ηA.","For commuting idempotents P_i, define E_ε=∏_i P_i^{ε_i}(I−P_i)^{1−ε_i}, ε∈{0,1}^m.","For a squarefree polynomial p(t)=∏_{λ∈S}(t−λ), Lagrange polynomials e_λ(t)=∏_{μ≠λ}(t−μ)/(λ−μ) define spectral projectors when p(T)=0."]
theorem_statement: If P_1,…,P_m are commuting idempotents on a finite-dimensional vector space, the E_ε are pairwise annihilating idempotents summing to I, and im(E_ε) is the simultaneous eigenspace P_i v=ε_i v. Hence the nonzero blocks give an exact direct-sum decomposition.
theorem_proof: All factors in E_ε commute, and each factor is idempotent, so E_ε²=E_ε. If ε≠δ, some index i has one product containing P_i and the other containing I−P_i. Their product is zero, proving E_εE_δ=0. Expanding ∏_i(P_i+(I−P_i)) gives Σ_εE_ε=I. Multiplication by P_i gives P_iE_ε=ε_iE_ε. Conversely, if v satisfies all simultaneous eigenvalue equations, every factor of E_ε acts as identity on v, so E_εv=v. Thus its image is exactly that eigenspace. Any v equals ΣE_εv; applying each projector to a supposed zero sum proves directness. The proof requires commutativity: arbitrary idempotents can have incompatible images and the product construction can fail even to be idempotent.

title: Symmetry as an action, representation and orbit calculation
central_question: What does a specified symmetry force, and which numerical features remain free after imposing it?
synopsis:
A symmetry label becomes mathematical information only after a group acts on a stated space. The collection repeatedly returns to Weyl groups, permutation characters, signed permutations, crystals and branching. These topics connect through invariant subspaces and orbit decompositions, not through shared large integers. The useful question is what the actual action fixes, which representations occur, and what independent parameters survive in the commuting algebra.

The elementary averaging projector is the organising construction. It turns a finite group action into an exact invariant subspace over a field where the group order is invertible. Character traces then measure multiplicities, and orbit splitting gives concrete restrictions and induced representations. Low-rank Weyl calculations provide a more structured version: a signed orbit sum becomes a polynomial identity after fixing the root coordinates and normalization. The A₂ denominator can be expanded completely; a nonconstant Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial requires its actual Bruhat interval and Hecke convention. Neither object is a universal score of computational complexity.

The signed-permutation examples are especially useful because they expose the limit of a symmetry inference. Over F₃, sign changes interchange the two nonzero entries, so the B₄ orbits are exactly the five Hamming-weight classes. Over the reals, invariance of a symmetric matrix under all independent sign changes kills off-diagonal entries, and permutation invariance makes its diagonal entries equal. This forces a scalar matrix on that irreducible coordinate representation, but two copies of a representation still admit independent scalar blocks and hence arbitrary positive frequency ratios. Symmetry narrows a model class; it need not pick a numerical constant, an empirical rank or a physical scale.

theorem_proof: For h∈G, ρ(h)R=|G|⁻¹Σ_gρ(hg)=R because left multiplication permutes G. Hence every vector in imR is invariant. If v is invariant then Rv=v, so imR=V^G and R²=R. The division hypothesis is essential; in characteristic dividing |G| this formula is unavailable and invariant functors need not be exact. For the orbit claim, every group element preserves the number of nonzero coordinates. Conversely, two vectors of equal weight can first have their supports matched by a coordinate permutation, then have their entries matched by sign changes, since F₃\{0}={1,−1}. Thus weight is a complete orbit invariant. Choose the support in binom(n,j) ways and independently choose each nonzero sign in 2^j ways. This proves both completeness and the sizes without enumerating all group elements.

title: Lie brackets, octonion associators and exceptional weight structure
central_question: Which identities survive a nonassociative or graded product, and what additional data turn exceptional dimensions into a Lie algebra?
synopsis:
This family joins two recurring themes: bracket consistency and exceptional symmetry. The starting point is a declared multiplication convention. Associative multiplication produces a commutator satisfying Jacobi; graded associative multiplication produces the super-Jacobi identity with parity signs. Octonionic multiplication is alternative rather than associative, so its commutator carries a nonzero Jacobiator. These are different algebraic structures, each with identities that can be derived and tested exactly.

The octonion model is especially productive because it turns regrouping into a measurable defect. Under a fixed Cayley–Dickson convention, the triple e₁,e₂,e₄ has associator 2e₇. Norm multiplicativity then yields a sharp universal bound for every triple, with a complete equality criterion. This gives a rigorous invariant of the multiplication, while preventing an illicit reassociation of three unrelated factors. The same discipline applies to superalgebras: in gl(1|1), the bracket of the two odd off-diagonal matrix units is an anticommutator and equals the identity, not an ordinary commutator.

Exceptional Lie algebras enter at the representation level. The decomposition so₁₆⊕S⁺ has dimension 120+128=248, and its D₈ roots together with the half-spin weights form the 240-element E₈ root set. That is a substantial and checkable weight calculation. It is still distinct from constructing the bracket: the so₁₆ action on S⁺ and an equivariant map Λ²S⁺→so₁₆ must be specified with a normalization satisfying spinor Jacobi. The magic-square dimension arithmetic likewise organises candidate structures without replacing their multiplication. This synthesis keeps the genuine exceptional mathematics while making its missing construction obligations visible.
definitions_json: ["Use quaternion units ij=k, jk=i, ki=j and octonion product (a,b)(c,d)=(ac−conj(d)b, da+b conj(c)).","The associator is [a,b,c]=(ab)c−a(bc); the octonion norm is multiplicative.","For homogeneous parity |X|∈{0,1}, [X,Y]_s=XY−(−1)^{|X||Y|}YX.","The E₈ root set is {±e_i±e_j:i<j} together with {(±1/2,…,±1/2):an even number of minus signs}."]
theorem_statement: For real octonions, ||(ab)c−a(bc)||≤2||a||||b||||c||. For nonzero norm product, equality holds exactly when (ab)c=−a(bc), and the constant two is sharp. Independently, the displayed E₈ root set has 240 vectors of squared length two.
theorem_proof: Write u=(ab)c and v=a(bc). Multiplicativity gives ||u||=||v||=n=||a||||b||||c||. Hence ||u−v||≤||u||+||v||=2n. If n>0, equality in the triangle inequality requires u and −v to have the same direction; equal norms make this exactly u=−v. The declared multiplication gives e₁e₂=e₃, e₃e₄=e₇, e₂e₄=e₆ and e₁e₆=−e₇, proving sharpness. For the root count, choosing two positions among eight and two independent signs gives 4·binom(8,2)=112 integer roots. Of the 2⁸ half-integral sign vectors exactly half have even parity: flipping one chosen sign pairs the two parity classes. Thus there are 128 such roots and 240 total. Each integer root has norm squared 1+1=2; each half-integral vector has 8/4=2. No Jacobi identity for an exceptional Lie bracket is implied by this count.

title: Local algebras, jets, path bases and structural flatness
central_question: How do relations determine a finite algebra, and which properties remain constant when those relations vary?
synopsis:
The local and quiver examples supply a concrete algebraic laboratory for the atlas. A finite Hilbert function is not determined by a few initial coefficients; it comes from the whole ideal. A constant vector-space dimension is not determined by a reported cochain profile; it comes from a basis or a locally free presentation. A symmetric Hilbert function is not enough to prove Gorenstein duality; the socle and multiplication pairing must be inspected. These distinctions turn several ambitious geometric discussions into tractable structural calculations.

The first model begins with two quadrics. An invertible change of coordinates converts them into u² and uv, revealing an infinite tail of powers of v. Adding cubic closure kills v³ and produces the intended four-dimensional algebra. Its basis gives the Hilbert function, radical powers and socle directly. The second model starts with a finite quiver and a square-zero loop. Path enumeration gives fourteen independent paths, and one projective relation removes exactly one dimension because its source and target prevent further left or right multiplication. The resulting rank thirteen is therefore uniform for a structural reason, not a sampling pattern.

These models also connect finite algebras to representation categories. Dual numbers and their matrix rings have different raw dimensions but equivalent module categories; radical layers and Ext groups retain structure that a state count misses. Conversely, a flat family can change Hochschild cohomology even while its basis size stays fixed. The family is organised so that basis certificates come first, module invariants second and deformation claims third. This ordering makes it possible to build interactive normal-form explorers without advertising an unimplemented general Gröbner, quiver-deformation or moduli solver.
definitions_json: ["For a graded algebra A, H_A(d)=dim_k A_d is its Hilbert function.","For a local Artinian algebra with maximal ideal m, soc(A)={a:ma=0}; a one-dimensional socle is required for the usual commutative Artinian Gorenstein condition.","A quiver path algebra has vertices as orthogonal idempotents and directed paths as a basis before imposing relations.","A finite algebra family is flat when its underlying module is locally free in the finite presentations used here; constant fibre dimension alone is not a general flatness proof."]
theorem_statement: Over any field, k[u,v]/(u²,uv,v³) has basis 1,u,v,v², Hilbert function (1,2,1), maximal ideal cube zero and socle span{u,v²}. The two quadratic relations alone give Hilbert function (1,2,1,1,…).
theorem_proof: The monomial ideal (u²,uv) kills exactly monomials divisible by u² or uv. Its surviving monomials are 1,u,v,v²,v³,…, so it has one surviving monomial in every degree at least two. Adding v³ kills all powers of v of degree at least three and leaves precisely 1,u,v,v². Their independence follows because a monomial ideal contains a polynomial exactly when each of its monomials belongs to the ideal. The maximal ideal is span{u,v,v²}; its square is span{v²} and its cube is zero. For a=a₀+a₁u+a₂v+a₃v², multiplication by u gives a₀u and multiplication by v gives a₀v+a₂v². Both vanish precisely when a₀=a₂=0. Hence the socle is span{u,v²}, of dimension two, and the algebra is not Gorenstein despite its symmetric Hilbert function. The coordinate change u=a−λb,v=b is invertible for every λ and turns (a²−λ²b²,ab−λb²) into (u²,uv), including in characteristic two.

Globally this is a nowhere-zero O(−1) subbundle in a trivial rank-two path summand; its quotient is O(1). The full path bundle is therefore O¹²⊕O(1), a locally free rank-thirteen module. title: Finite operator algebras, modular flow and equilibrium
central_question: What do a faithful state and its dynamics determine exactly in a finite algebra?
synopsis:
The operator-algebra discussions become most transparent when the algebra, state and representation are separated. In M_d(C), a faithful state is given by a positive density matrix ρ. It defines expectations on observables, an inner-product geometry on matrix space and a modular flow. A thermal Hamiltonian H defines another flow through conjugation. A Gibbs state links the two with a temperature-dependent rescaling and sign, but the state Hamiltonian −logρ is not the same object as the standard-form modular generator acting on matrices.

This distinction is one of the strongest connections across the later years. On the Hilbert space of Hilbert–Schmidt matrices, left multiplication represents the observable algebra and right multiplication represents its commutant. The modular operator is Δ=L_ρR_{ρ⁻¹}. Its eigenvalues on matrix units are ratios p_i/p_j, so its generator has spectral gaps rather than the original energy levels. A second faithful state produces a unitary relative cocycle with a twisted multiplication law. These are exact finite models of powerful general constructions, with all domains automatic and every formula inspectable.

Equilibrium also requires a declared dynamics convention. With α_t(A)=e^{itH}Ae^{−itH}, the Gibbs state satisfies φ(Aα_{iβ}(B))=φ(BA). The boundary identity follows from cyclicity of trace and extends to all matrices because finite-dimensional imaginary-time conjugation is entire. This offers a meaningful interactive calculation: change populations, inspect modular frequencies and test the KMS relation. It does not turn a fitted ratio q=e^{−βE} into a deformed quantum group, or establish infinite type-III modular inclusions, holographic identities or geometric field equations.

theorem_statement: For Ω=ρ^{1/2}, the Tomita map S(AΩ)=A*Ω satisfies S=JΔρ^{1/2}. If ρ=Z⁻¹e^{−βH}, φ is α-invariant and obeys the stated KMS identity. The modular generator −logΔρ has eigenvalues log(p_j/p_i) on E_ij.
theorem_proof: Every matrix X can be written Aρ^{1/2} because ρ is invertible. Therefore S(X)=(Xρ^{−1/2})*ρ^{1/2}=ρ^{−1/2}X*ρ^{1/2}. Meanwhile Δρ^{1/2}X=ρ^{1/2}Xρ^{−1/2}; applying J gives exactly the same expression. In a ρ-eigenbasis, ΔρE_ij=(p_i/p_j)E_ij, yielding the generator formula by finite functional calculus. For KMS, α_{iβ}(B)=e^{−βH}Be^{βH}. Multiply φ(Aα_{iβ}B) by Z and cyclically move the final e^{βH} to the front: tr(e^{−βH}Ae^{−βH}Be^{βH})=tr(Ae^{−βH}B)=tr(e^{−βH}BA). Division by Z proves the identity. Since ρ commutes with e^{itH}, cyclicity also proves φ(α_tA)=φ(A). Positivity and normalization follow directly from ρ≥0 and trρ=1.

title: Universal constructions, quotients and equivalence
central_question: Which maps descend through a quotient, and which reversible constructions preserve the whole mathematical problem?
synopsis:
The categorical thread becomes strongest when a named operation is replaced by a construction with a testable mapping property. A quotient first declares which distinctions are erased. A pushout identifies two copies of shared data. An adjunction converts one kind of mapping problem into another, while an equivalence supplies inverse functors and natural comparison maps. These statements organize mathematics across the archive because they separate an object from a chosen presentation and make compatibility part of the theorem. They also distinguish several levels of preservation: agreement of dimensions is weaker than an isomorphism, an isomorphism of individual objects is weaker than a natural equivalence, and an equivalence of categories must respect the specified morphisms.

The useful starting point is the category of linear dynamical systems. An object is a vector space with an endomorphism A; a morphism L satisfies LA=BL. This single equation guarantees L exp(tA)=exp(tB)L by the power series, so composition preserves dynamics rather than merely relabeling coordinates. The tensor–Hom correspondence then makes composition of structures explicit. Currying is available for arbitrary algebraic vector spaces, whereas a duality datum with coevaluation requires finite dimension. This distinction prevents an infinite formal basis sum from being treated as an algebraic tensor. Reconstruction has a similar demand: a finite group can be recovered from the natural automorphisms of the forgetful functor on all finite G-sets, using the regular G-set and its equivariant maps; one representation or one dimension table cannot carry the same information.

An adjunction instead supplies natural bijections of Hom sets, with unit and counit satisfying the triangle identities.","In algebraic vector spaces, a duality datum ev:W⊗V→k and coev:k→V⊗W must reconstruct every vector through both triangle identities. Every algebraic tensor is a finite sum."]

theorem_proof: Given compatible maps u:B→V and v:C→V with ui=vj, the map (b,c)↦u(b)+v(c) kills every (i(a),−j(a)). It therefore descends uniquely to P because the quotient map is surjective. Conversely every map from P gives such a compatible pair by composition. Rank-nullity gives the dimension formula, including the correction needed when both legs have a common kernel. For finite-dimensional V choose a basis e_r and its dual basis; coev(1)=Σe_r⊗e^r and evaluation give v=Σe^r(v)e_r. Conversely, if coev(1)=Σ_{r=1}^n v_r⊗w_r, one triangle identity writes every v as Σv_r ev(w_r⊗v). Thus finitely many v_r span V. This proves the finite-dimensional necessity directly, rather than inferring duality from an informal adjunction symbol.

title: Chain complexes, exactness and certificates of equivalence
central_question: How can a reduction preserve homology, and what finite identities certify that nothing essential was lost?
synopsis:
A chain complex records permitted boundaries and the relations among them. Its defining equation d²=0 is the first useful certificate: every boundary is a cycle, so a quotient of cycles by boundaries exists. The archive repeatedly approaches more elaborate constructions through this same requirement. Total complexes need Koszul signs; mapping cones need a genuine chain map; a blocked representation needs maps and a chain homotopy before it can inherit the original cohomology. These are constructive conditions. They provide explicit witnesses that a smaller calculation preserves the invariant instead of only producing similar output on an example.

The key distinction is between changing a presentation and changing an object. Adding a contractible pair increases the number of coordinates while preserving homology. Consequently total chain dimension cannot define an invariant of the derived object. Conversely a cochain map can annihilate a nonzero class, so the fact that an operation is linear or functorial does not prove that it preserves obstruction spaces. The finite Hodge decomposition gives a third view: with declared positive inner products, harmonic vectors represent homology, but that representative depends on the metric while the quotient space is invariant under chain equivalence. The supertrace index then becomes an exact cancellation statement, because all nonzero differential modes occur in paired even and odd degrees. No asymptotic heat approximation is required in the finite model.

theorem_proof: For a cocycle c, the contraction identity gives c−ip(c)=d h(c), hence the classes of c and ip(c) agree. Since pi=Id, the induced maps are inverse. In a bicomplex the two mixed compositions have coefficients (−1)^p and (−1)^{p+1}; they cancel because the raw differentials commute. The remaining squares are zero. title: Derived products, extension classes and deformation obstructions
central_question: What information survives in Tor, Ext and a tangent complex that an ordinary product or dimension count discards?
synopsis:
Derived constructions retain the effect of relations that ordinary algebra has suppressed. Tensoring a resolution and applying Hom to it produce Tor and Ext; these groups measure failures of exactness rather than furnishing decorative refinements of a product. A particular extension belongs to an Ext group, so the dimension of the ambient group cannot determine whether that extension splits. Likewise a nonzero obstruction space is a location where an obstruction may live, not a proof that every first-order motion fails. The actual class or nonlinear obstruction map must be computed.

This principle unifies three distinct lines of the source corpus. Dual numbers provide an exact module model with nonzero derived tensor groups in all positive degrees. A singular hypersurface supplies an explicit cotangent complex and a failed second-order lift. A differential graded Lie algebra organizes nonlinear compatibility through the Maurer–Cartan equation. These constructions share a mechanism: solve at first order, identify the next defect as a cocycle, and ask whether a correcting term makes it a boundary. Their coefficient rings and degree conventions remain different. A deformation of a scheme, an extension of modules and a flatness problem for an algebra must therefore be connected by an actual functor or comparison theorem before their obstruction groups are identified. The archive’s elliptic self-extension example is especially useful as a boundary: stable objects can have nontrivial self-extensions, whereas an honestly semisimple abelian category has none in positive Ext degree.

theorem_proof: The resolution is exact because the kernel and image of multiplication by ε are both εR. Tensoring it with k makes every differential zero, as does applying Hom_R(−,k), proving the Tor and Ext assertions. An R-linear section of R→k would send 1 to a vector v with εv=0, hence v∈εR, whose quotient is zero; it cannot map back to 1. The next equation is solvable precisely when this cocycle class vanishes, which is a class-level criterion.

title: Filtrations, spectral sequences and information at infinity
central_question: How much of a total object can be recovered from graded pages, truncations and inverse systems?
synopsis:
A filtration is an organized sequence of partial views. Passing to the associated graded records the layers but suppresses how they interact. A spectral sequence progressively restores some of that interaction through differentials. Even after every differential is determined, reconstructing an integral group or ring can require extension and multiplicative data. The source sequence develops this distinction through fibrations, filtered complexes, cohomological shifts and inverse limits. Their common question is not whether the displayed table looks plausible, but which connecting maps remain unknown.

The Hopf fibration and the product S²×S¹ have the same initial Serre page but different transgressions. The finite model below makes the same phenomenon an exact two-coordinate computation. It also exposes a second loss: Z/4 and Z/2⊕Z/2 have the same two graded layers, although only the former has an element of order four. A filtration therefore supports a partial reconstruction interface, with each unknown differential and extension listed as an unresolved input. Perverse shifts and t-structures add a related bookkeeping lesson. The declaration of a heart or a support/cosupport condition changes which cohomological degrees count as an object; it is not recoverable from an unshifted label. Finally an infinite inverse system has genuinely limiting information. The doubling tower of integers has vanishing ordinary inverse limit but a nonzero derived limit; no finite truncation alone certifies that infinite result. These examples justify a hierarchy of outputs: graded dimensions, actual graded groups, filtered groups, rings, and geometric objects.

title: Spaces, chains, torsion and refined homology
central_question: Which features belong to the space, which to its cell structure, and which survive a change of coefficients?
synopsis:
The topological material repeatedly becomes more informative after the underlying space is specified. A triangle can mean three vertices, its three-edge boundary, or a filled two-simplex. These objects have different chain groups and therefore different homology. A graph drawn on a torus is still a one-dimensional complex until its faces are attached; its cycle rank need not equal the surface’s first Betti number. Polyhedral spheres have the same homology while retaining different symmetry groups. These examples teach how to ask a sharper classification question: first choose the equivalence relation, then ask which invariant can distinguish its classes.

Integer coefficients add a second layer. Rational homology records free rank and erases torsion, so it cannot distinguish every space or quotient. A Smith normal form supplies an exact arithmetic certificate for the torsion, provided row and column operations are unimodular and the relevant quotient is actually the homology group. Reduced homology removes the connected-component contribution in degree zero; intersection homology instead restricts which chains may meet singular strata. The two operations address different questions. The cone on a torus is contractible as an ordinary space, yet lower-middle allowable chains retain two one-dimensional classes because their potential cone fillings meet the forbidden apex. A refinement is useful precisely because its allowed chains and intended invariance are explicit, rather than because the word cohomology was attached to a construction.

title: Persistent topology, interleavings and random birth laws
central_question: How does a topological feature persist through a filtration, and what perturbation or randomness can be certified?
synopsis:
Persistence studies a sequence of spaces together with the maps between them. A barcode records the life of a class, including classes that disappear before the terminal space is reached. This is why the colimit cannot replace a persistence module: a finite bar contributes information during its lifetime even though its eventual image is zero. The archive moves from explicit small filtrations to diagram distances, stability and random birth times. These developments fit one constructive interface: input a legal filtration, compute boundary maps and induced maps on homology, and then declare which comparison theorem applies.

The legal-filtration requirement is essential. A simplex cannot enter before one of its faces. Assigning a dramatic label such as singularity or cavity to a parameter value does not change homology; the chain complex changes when cells or maps change. A metric between persistence diagrams also needs the diagonal. An unmatched point can die by matching to its closest diagonal point, with cost half its lifetime in the usual ℓ∞ convention. Stability then has an exact elementary core: uniformly close functions give mutually shifted sublevel inclusions. Passing to barcode stability adds finiteness or tameness assumptions. Random filtrations supply another useful bridge, because a feature born when all required edges are present has a birth time given by a maximum of random variables. This connects a topological lifetime to an exact order-statistic law without claiming that all random topology reduces to one scalar distribution.

A point (b,d) has diagonal cost (d−b)/2.","For functions f,g on one space, their sublevel filtrations are F_t={f≤t}, G_t={g≤t}. A uniform bound ||f−g||∞≤ε gives an ε-interleaving by inclusions."]

For a square whose four edge times are independent uniform variables on [0,1] and whose face enters at one, its H₁ birth B has P(B≤t)=t⁴ and expected lifetime 1/5.
theorem_proof: Before time one the triangle has three components; at one its edge boundary matrix has rank two, merging them and leaving the one-dimensional cycle kernel. At two the face boundary spans that kernel. This proves the bars, including the two simultaneous deaths. For the random square, the unique graph cycle exists exactly when every edge has arrived, so B=max(U₁,U₂,U₃,U₄). Independence gives P(B≤t)=∏P(U_j≤t)=t⁴. This is the direct interleaving certificate before any diagram theorem is invoked.

title: Local-to-global gluing, cellular sheaves and Hodge obstructions
central_question: When can compatible local data be replaced by one global object, and how can the obstruction be calculated exactly?
synopsis:
Gluing is a mapping problem with two distinct outcomes. A sheaf axiom says a compatible family glues uniquely; it does not say every arbitrary family is compatible or that higher cohomology vanishes. The circle examples make this distinction concrete. Two arcs overlap in two components, allowing two discrepancies; local constants can change both discrepancies only by the same amount. Their difference is therefore a one-dimensional global obstruction. This is an exact finite complex with a transparent quotient, not a violation of sheaf gluing.

The same mechanism extends to graph potentials, cellular sheaves and discrete Hodge theory. Edge values are globally integrable exactly when their cycle sums vanish. A spanning tree constructs the potential, while each remaining edge checks one cycle constraint. With matrix or scalar transport, the coefficient system changes the equation itself; the ordinary cycle of the underlying graph need not yield a nonzero sheaf class. A rank-one local system on a circle has cohomology controlled by its total monodromy. Its harmonic representative is then a metric-dependent choice inside a metric-independent quotient. This is especially relevant to source claims based on residuals: a vector with zero Hodge Laplacian residual may be a nonzero harmonic obstruction. Certifying H¹=0 requires a rank or coercivity statement on the entire relevant space, not one successful vector. Transfers between local models similarly need a chain equivalence before they can transport obstruction classes bijectively.

In a higher-dimensional cellular sheaf, face-composition identities must additionally make δ²=0; arbitrary transport matrices alone do not guarantee a complex.

title: Periods, cocycles, winding and characteristic classes
central_question: Which global defects survive changes of local choices, and what makes their values topological?
synopsis:
A cocycle expresses consistency of repeated composition; a coboundary expresses a defect removable by changing local choices. Periods and characteristic classes provide ways to detect what remains. The archive contains several versions: winding of a nonvanishing loop, projective phases of group actions, transition functions of bundles and characteristic-form integrals. They share an invariance mechanism, but their coefficients, degrees and products differ. A useful synthesis keeps the actual equation visible rather than treating every nonzero loop quantity as the same obstruction.

Winding is protected by avoidance of the origin: a continuous nonvanishing loop has an integer degree, and a homotopy through nonvanishing loops preserves it. A curl flux is instead a boundary integral depending continuously on the field; equality for two surfaces with the same boundary is a Stokes statement, not automatic quantization. Group projective phases satisfy a two-cocycle equation because multiplication is associative. Rephasing the operators changes the cocycle by a coboundary, while the commutator phase for a commuting pair is unchanged. Bundle transition functions obey their own triple-overlap identity, and characteristic forms connect curvature to integral topology only for a declared bundle and normalization. The source corpus’s four-torus example makes the latter quantitative: if c₁=n dx₁∧dx₂+m dx₃∧dx₄ on the unit torus, then ∫c₁²=2nm, with the factor two arising from degree-two commutativity. A topological density can have a variation that is entirely a boundary term, so it need not furnish a bulk field equation.

The alternating commutator ratio therefore detects the nontrivial projective class and survives rephasing. For the angular form, differentiation gives zero on the punctured plane. Restrict to the unit circle x=cos t,y=sin t: the form becomes dt and its integral is 2π. Every globally exact form has zero integral on a closed loop by the fundamental theorem, proving nonexactness. This is the same local-to-global pattern as gluing, with a de Rham coefficient model rather than finite incidence coordinates.

title: Metrics, curvature, scale and transport geometry
central_question: Which conclusions follow from a declared metric, and which survive a change of scale or representation?
synopsis:
Geometry begins with enough data to measure. A coordinate chart does not select a Riemannian metric, a positive symmetric weight table need not satisfy the triangle inequality, and a Jacobian alone does not determine singular values without input and output inner products. These distinctions let the metric material in the archive be organized by constructive outputs: path length, geodesics, curvature, volume growth and transport distance. The archive’s hyperbolic examples are particularly coherent because the metric is explicit and each claimed phenomenon can be computed from it.

On the upper half-plane with ds²=(dx²+dy²)/y², the connection, vertical unit-speed geodesics and curvature −1 agree with the disk model under the Cayley map. Constant metric rescaling changes distances, volumes, curvature and Laplace spectra in related but distinct ways. This blocks a common confusion between a geometric normalization and a dimensionless threshold. Hyperbolic volume growth gives another exact boundary: local Euclidean behavior does not imply a global doubling bound. Discrete Ollivier curvature introduces still another metric construction, comparing probability distributions by optimal transport. Its value depends on the measure convention as well as the graph, and it cannot certify unrelated computational hardness. Prefix ultrametrics supply a complementary geometry: distance is controlled by the first differing digit, while a many-to-one real coding map can erase prefix information through carries. The best synthesis therefore treats metrics as inputs whose consequences can be tested, rather than as labels attached to algebraic expressions.

title: Hamiltonian, symplectic and contact structures
central_question: How do conservation, reduction and projection follow from a specified geometric form?
synopsis:
Symplectic geometry makes dynamical rules structural: a nondegenerate closed two-form converts the derivative of a Hamiltonian into a vector field. Contact geometry replaces this even-dimensional structure with a maximally nonintegrable hyperplane distribution in odd dimension. The archive’s examples become coherent when these forms are written before their consequences. Hamiltonian conservation follows from antisymmetry, a Casimir is a much stronger object, and a cyclic coordinate can be removed only after its conjugate momentum is fixed. A dimension count for a quotient needs a regular constraint and a free action, not just a formal subtraction.

The oscillator links Hamilton’s equations, Hamilton–Jacobi graphs and Riccati evolution without identifying their coordinate descriptions. Its full phase-space flow is smooth for all times. The generating function for the image of one initial graph fails at a caustic because projection to configuration space ceases to be invertible. The divergence is in the graph representation rather than in the trajectory itself. The quiver-style cotangent quotient supplies an equally concrete reduction: solving a moment-map equation and quotienting a free scaling action produces cotangent coordinates, including their canonical one-form. Contact examples then add a compatible but distinct structure. A Legendrian curve satisfies a tangent condition such as dz−y dx=0; on a thermodynamic equilibrium surface the same contact logic yields a potential identity and a Maxwell relation, provided the stated differentiability and change of variables hold.

A Legendrian submanifold has dimension n and tangent bundle inside kerα."]

Quotienting removes that kernel and leaves a nondegenerate form. The restricted H is independent of q₂, so it descends; the projected full equations are exactly Hamilton’s equations of H_μ. In a chart z₁=1 with z=(1,u), the constraint gives w=(−up,p) and the canonical one-form w·dz is p du.

title: Connections, gauge covariance, curvature and holonomy
central_question: How can local transport and global loop effects be distinguished and checked without confusing flatness with triviality?
synopsis:
A connection supplies a rule for differentiating and transporting sections. Curvature measures its local failure to commute in two independent directions; holonomy measures transport around a loop. They interact, but neither is interchangeable with the other or with the topology of the underlying space. A one-dimensional circle supports no curvature two-form and can still have nontrivial monodromy. On a simply connected surface, a nonflat connection can have loop holonomy arising from curvature even when the bundle is topologically trivial. A nontrivial bundle can additionally obstruct a global gauge potential. These distinctions give the archive’s connection and Berry material a common, precise architecture.

Gauge transformations change coordinates in the fibers. They conjugate loop holonomy at its base point, leaving conjugacy-invariant information such as trace, determinant and eigenvalues unchanged. The ordered product matters for matrices; scalar circulation cannot stand in for a nonabelian calculation. The source’s nilpotent shear example is especially effective because its exponentials terminate and its loop product is an exact polynomial. Berry transport adds a geometric realization: eigenlines form a bundle over a parameter space, and local eigenvector choices are gauge choices. A Chern number requires that declared bundle and a normalized curvature integral; it cannot be recovered from a phase function on an unidentified state space. For the spin-half sphere example the integral is one, proving that no globally smooth potential can represent that curvature on the whole sphere.

Ordered loop holonomy is the composite returning to its base fiber.","Flat means F=0. Trivial holonomy means every relevant loop acts as identity. Topological triviality means the underlying bundle has a global trivialization; these are different properties."]

Each interior h_j⁻¹ cancels its neighboring h_j, leaving only h₀Hh₀⁻¹; this proves gauge covariance and explains why entries themselves are not invariant. Since X²=Y²=0, exp(xX)=I+xX and exp(yY)=I+yY exactly. Multiplying the four factors gives the displayed polynomial, whose determinant is one and trace is 2+x²y². Setting x=y=ε yields I+ε²[X,Y] plus explicit cubic and quartic terms. This is the exact algebraic mechanism behind a small plaquette limit; a smooth curvature interpretation additionally needs specified base directions, derivative terms and a transport sign convention. On a circle A=iα dθ is flat by dimension, but with parallel transport defined by s′+iαs=0 its holonomy is exp(−2πiα), nontrivial for noninteger α. Thus flatness alone does not force global trivial monodromy.

title: Curves, moving frames and geometric variational models
central_question: Which curve geometry is fixed by curvature, and when does a variational principle actually select a shape?
synopsis:
Curves provide a manageable laboratory for separating geometry, coordinates and dynamics. An affine transformation composes by the semidirect rule, while a time-dependent coordinate frame adds velocity and acceleration terms. A Frenet frame follows a curve’s tangent, normal and binormal; its rotation can be written using a Darboux angular-velocity vector. Neither operation by itself is a new physical law. The archive’s most useful curve examples become explicit once the parameter, regularity and objective are fixed: winding requires a nonvanishing loop, spirograph closure requires commensurate frequencies, and a clothoid minimizes one declared curvature-rate energy with endpoint curvatures.

The variational distinction is especially important. Minimizing the squared derivative of curvature under fixed endpoint curvatures selects linear curvature, but prescribing endpoint positions and tangent directions adds integral constraints and changes the admissible problem. A clothoid is therefore an exact solution of a clearly stated functional, not a universal optimal connector. Extrinsic surface geometry makes a parallel point about normalization: if mean curvature is the average of the principal curvatures, a round sphere has Willmore energy 4π at every radius; using their sum changes the scale by four. Surface immersion, embedding and eversion are also different questions. The curve and surface material consequently contributes a practical discipline: identify the geometric object, pick invariant quantities, state the boundary data and only then optimize or classify.

It describes the same frame rotation rather than an additional dynamical postulate.

title: Transforms, frames and cancellation in a declared norm
central_question: When do coefficients preserve information, and how does the chosen measure control a reconstruction error?
synopsis: The recurring analytical object is a map from functions or vectors to coefficients. Fourier, Haar, wavelet, shearlet and character systems make different geometries visible, but every useful reconstruction statement has an ambient space, a normalization and a completeness hypothesis. The early Bessel–Parseval and Hardy–BMO questions already distinguish coefficient energy from the energy of the original object. Later sampling, weighted atoms and coherence questions add perturbations and observation loss. These are constructive ingredients for an analysis workflow: first identify which subspace the coefficients see, then calculate its norm identity or frame bounds, and finally account for noise and discarded directions. A finite example is valuable because every coefficient and residual can be inspected exactly. It does not automatically establish a continuous transform theorem or a global sampling theorem.

Expanding ||P_mx+r||² removes the cross term, and orthonormality evaluates the projection norm as the sum of coefficient squares. title: Analytic domains, contour certificates and positive spectral functions
central_question: What information is certified by local analytic data, and which global conclusions require a domain or positivity theorem?
synopsis: Analytic reasoning becomes especially effective when its domain is part of the input. Cauchy integrals extract coefficients only when the disk and singularity assumptions hold. Logarithmic derivatives locate zeros and poles locally but also carry branch and continuation data. A contour argument counts zeros with multiplicity; it need not show that two counted zeros coincide. The 2026 phase and positive-atom discussions add a useful constructive class: a rational function built from positive real atoms has a fixed imaginary sign and strictly ordered real zeros. That model connects coefficient extraction, monotonicity and spectral measures without making any claim about an unspecified zeta operator. It also provides a small exact laboratory in which poles, residues, roots and signs can all be checked.
definitions_json: ["A holomorphic function is complex differentiable on an open set. Cauchy extraction on |z−a|=r requires holomorphy on a neighborhood of the closed disk.","A Herglotz function maps the upper half-plane into itself. For distinct real t_j and positive μ_j, M(z)=Σ_j μ_j/(t_j−z) is a rational example.","The argument principle counts zeros minus poles inside a contour that avoids both; the count includes multiplicity."]
theorem_statement: For t₁<⋯<t_m and μ_j>0, M(z)=Σ μ_j/(t_j−z) is Herglotz. On every interval (t_j,t_{j+1}) it is strictly increasing from −∞ to +∞ and therefore has exactly one simple zero. Its poles are simple with residues −μ_j.
theorem_proof: Write z=x+iy with y>0. The imaginary part of 1/(t−z) is y/((t−x)²+y²)>0; positive weighted summation proves the half-plane property. For real x away from the poles, M′(x)=Σ μ_j/(t_j−x)²>0. Immediately to the right of t_j its own term tends to −∞, and immediately to the left of t_{j+1} that pole contributes +∞. Continuity and the intermediate value theorem give a zero, strict monotonicity gives uniqueness, and a positive derivative at that zero makes it simple. Multiplying the jth term by z−t_j and taking the limit gives residue −μ_j. Outside the extreme poles all denominators have the same sign, so no further real zero occurs. The argument proves the entire finite interlacing structure without plotting a dense scatter of points. A difference of two such functions does not preserve positive weights and has to be reanalyzed. Separately, the contour integral f^(n)(a)=n!/(2πi)∮f(z)/(z−a)^(n+1)dz follows by the convergent Taylor expansion on a smaller disk and termwise integration; its size bound is n!M/r^n. These two exact mechanisms explain why sign, locality and the contour hypothesis should travel with any calculated residue or root count.
