title: Exact integrals, special functions and normalized periods
central_question: How can an integral be reduced to an exact constant while keeping convergence, branch and normalization information visible?
synopsis: The archive contains a sustained exact-integration strand: elementary logarithmic moments, sine quotients, Catalan and dilogarithm values, theta and modular transformations, Mellin central values, elliptic logarithms and a final finite-phase integral. These belong together as calculational methods rather than as one claimed transcendence theory. A useful reduction identifies an integration domain, a convergent expansion, the interchange theorem and a final finite or controlled infinite expression. The resulting number can then be checked independently by rational recurrences, symmetry or tail enclosures. The elementary Mellin moment below is a central reusable example. It supplies factorial weights exactly and explains why positive geometric expansions turn certain logarithmic integrals into zeta sums. More elaborate modular and elliptic examples retain additional transformation and branch information that this elementary calculation does not replace.
definitions_json: ["For a>0 and integer m≥0, the Mellin logarithmic moment is J_m(a)=∫₀¹x^(a−1)(−log x)^m dx.","An exact special-function identity includes its parameter region and branch convention. A numerical agreement at one parameter is a check, not the identity itself.","A period representation here means a specified convergent integral or analytic continuation; no algebraic independence claim follows from that name."]
theorem_statement: For real a>0 and integer m≥0, J_m(a)=m!/a^(m+1). For m≥1, ∫₀¹(−log x)^m/(1−x) dx=m!ζ(m+1). Truncating the latter positive series after n=N leaves a tail between zero and (m!/m)N^(−m).
theorem_proof: Set x=e^(−t). Then dx=−e^(−t)dt and x^(a−1)dx=−e^(−at)dt, so the first integral becomes ∫₀∞e^(−at)t^m dt. The substitution u=at factors out a^(−m−1). Integration by parts gives Γ(m+1)=mΓ(m), starting from Γ(1)=1; the boundary terms vanish because an exponential dominates any fixed power. This proves the first formula and convergence at both endpoints. For 0<x<1, 1/(1−x)=Σ_{k≥0}x^k. All summands multiplied by (−log x)^m are nonnegative, so monotone convergence justifies exchanging integral and sum without an unproved uniform bound near x=1. Each resulting moment is m!/(k+1)^(m+1). The series converges exactly for m≥1 in the nonnegative-integer range. The tail is m!Σ_{n>N}n^(−m−1), at most m!∫_N∞t^(−m−1)dt=(m!/m)N^(−m). The m=0 integral diverges logarithmically, showing why the endpoint restriction is mathematical content. Complex a or a noninteger logarithmic exponent can be handled only after choosing powers and checking a new convergence region. This proof is deliberately transparent enough that its finite partial sums and error bounds can be reproduced with rational arithmetic.

title: Self-adjoint spectra, heat traces and spectral dimension
central_question: What does a spectrum actually determine, and which operator-domain and multiplicity data are needed before using it?
synopsis: The spectral strand moves from concrete Jacobi and Toeplitz matrices to unbounded operators, residual estimates, heat traces, zeta transforms and spectral dimensions. Its organizing object is not a free-standing list of eigenvalues but an operator with a domain and a functional calculus. Self-adjointness makes a residual meaningful as distance to the spectrum; nonnormal matrices behave differently. Multiplicities change counting functions and commutants even when a list of distinct eigenvalues looks unchanged. Fixed-time trace class is also distinct from short-time heat asymptotics. A diagonal Hilbert-space model makes all these distinctions constructive and supplies a precise bridge between counting growth, heat decay and a zeta convergence half-plane. It is an exact model, not a proposed identification with zeros of a number-theoretic function.
definitions_json: ["On ℓ²(N), define Ae_n=n²e_n with domain D(A)={x:Σn⁴|x_n|²<∞}. This domain makes A self-adjoint and nonnegative.","The counting function with multiplicity is N_A(Λ)=#{n:n²≤Λ}. The heat operator H_t=e^(−tA) has diagonal entries e^(−tn²).","The spectral zeta series is ζ_A(s)=Σn^(−2s), initially defined where it converges absolutely."]
theorem_statement: For the specified A, N_A(Λ)=⌊√Λ⌋ for Λ≥1, H_t is trace class for every t>0, and √t Tr(H_t)→√π/2 as t↓0. The defining zeta series converges absolutely exactly when Re s>1/2. Its positive heat trace obeys ∫₁∞e^(−tx²)dx≤Σ_{n≥1}e^(−tn²)≤∫₀∞e^(−tx²)dx.
theorem_proof: Coordinatewise multiplication by a real sequence is self-adjoint on its maximal square-summability domain; equivalently the adjoint condition forces the same weighted square sum. Its resolvent at −1 has diagonal entries 1/(n²+1), and finite coordinate truncations converge in operator norm because the remaining supremum tends to zero. Thus the resolvent is compact. The counting identity is immediate from n²≤Λ. For t>0, the diagonal entries of H_t are positive and summable by the integral test, so its trace equals their sum. The function x↦e^(−tx²) decreases on [0,∞); rectangle comparison gives the two integral bounds. Their difference is at most ∫₀¹1 dx=1. Multiplying by √t and substituting u=√t x makes both bounds tend to ∫₀∞e^(−u²)du=√π/2. This proves the leading heat asymptotic without asserting an unproved full expansion. Finally the absolute zeta series is Σn^(−2Re s), and the p-series test gives precisely Re s>1/2. Repeating every eigenvalue n times would instead give N(Λ) of order Λ and heat growth of order t^(−1), so multiplicity changes the inferred dimension. The proof exposes where positivity, compactness and the actual counting law enter.

title: Evolution equations through conservation and energy
central_question: Which quantities are transported, conserved or dissipated by the stated evolution law and boundary conditions?
synopsis: Heat, nonlinear waves, reaction–diffusion and gradient flows recur across the four years. The useful common language is an evolution equation accompanied by a balance law. A conserved mass and a decreasing energy are different statements: a reaction term can destroy the first, and changing the metric of a gradient flow changes the second. Spatial boundary conditions determine whether integration by parts closes the calculation. The simplest periodic heat equation supplies a complete constructive model with a solution formula, a conserved mean and a quantitative decay estimate for every nonconstant Fourier mode. The nonlinear wave and Cahn–Hilliard members then show how the same workflow changes with the equation. An explicit profile must be substituted into that equation, rather than recognized by its shape.
definitions_json: ["On the circle x∈[0,2π], let u_t=κu_xx with κ>0 and periodic boundary conditions. Its spatial mean is ū=(2π)^(−1)∫u dx.","The fluctuation energy is E(t)=½∫|u−ū|²dx. For sufficiently regular u, integration by parts has no boundary contribution.","A gradient flow is defined by both an energy functional and a metric or mobility operator; L² and H^(−1) gradient flows need not conserve the same quantities."]
theorem_statement: Periodic heat flow conserves the mean and satisfies E′=−κ∫|u_x|²dx≤−2κE. Consequently ||u(t)−ū||₂≤e^(−κt)||u(0)−ū||₂. For a Fourier mode cos(nx), the decay rate is exactly κn².
theorem_proof: Integrating the PDE over one period yields d∫u/dt=κ[u_x]₀^(2π)=0, so the mean is constant. Differentiating E and integrating by parts gives E′=κ∫(u−ū)u_xx dx=−κ∫u_x²dx for a real solution; the complex case uses the real part. Expand the mean-zero fluctuation in Fourier modes. Parseval gives ∫|u_x|²=2πΣ_{n≠0}n²|û_n|²≥2πΣ_{n≠0}|û_n|²=2E. This Poincaré inequality yields E′≤−2κE; multiplying by e^(2κt) and integrating proves the stated norm estimate. Each Fourier coefficient solves û_n′=−κn²û_n, giving the exact mode formula and a spectral construction of the solution. For rough L² data, approximate by finite Fourier sums, apply the same inequality, and pass to the L² limit. This argument also exhibits its boundary dependence. For Cahn–Hilliard, u_t=Δμ with μ=δE/δu, the analogous calculation gives E′=−∫|∇μ|² and a conserved mean. For the L² flow u_t=−μ it instead gives E′=−∫μ², usually with no mass conservation. Naming an energy without specifying the mobility would miss this distinction.

title: Discretization, truncation and controlled approximation
central_question: Which finite approximation preserves the model’s invariants, and what bound connects it to the intended continuous object?
synopsis: Approximation becomes usable when its error sources are separated and bounded. The archive includes positive diffusion stencils, CFL conditions, distributed halo exchange, lattice anisotropy, FFT differentiation, Newton error and inverse cutoffs. They share a need to distinguish consistency from stability and implementation correctness. A correct communication pattern cannot repair an unstable time step; a stable matrix cannot recover frequencies never observed. The periodic heat stencil below has sharp positivity conditions, exact mass conservation and an explicit Fourier symbol. It is therefore a fully inspectable worked model. Its continuum error additionally needs smoothness and a consistency estimate. The inverse-cutoff lab L04 uses a different, explicitly declared observation model: bias decreases with cutoff while noise amplification increases. The common capability is selecting a finite scale under a proved error budget, not one universal algorithm.

Fixed-grid identities use the sum-of-squares norm; continuum error rates use the normalized norm (N^(−1)Σ|u_j|²)^(1/2).","Consistency compares the discrete equation with a sufficiently smooth exact solution; it is distinct from finite-dimensional conservation and positivity."]
theorem_statement: T_r preserves Σu_j for every r. It preserves nonnegativity exactly for 0≤r≤1/2. In that range it contracts the discrete ℓ² norm, with Fourier amplification 1−4r sin²(πk/N). For a smooth heat solution, the forward-Euler centered-space residual is O(Δt+Δx²) on a fixed bounded time interval with bounded derivatives.
theorem_proof: Cyclic summation makes each old value appear with coefficient r+(1−2r)+r=1, proving mass conservation. If all three coefficients are nonnegative, every new coordinate is a convex combination. Conversely a coordinate basis vector detects a negative off-diagonal coefficient when r<0 or a negative central coefficient when r>1/2, proving the sharp positivity condition. Convexity of z↦|z|² then gives |(T_ru)_j|²≤r|u_(j−1)|²+(1−2r)|u_j|²+r|u_(j+1)|². Sum over j to get contraction. Substituting the discrete character e^(2πikj/N) gives the amplification symbol r e^(−2πik/N)+(1−2r)+r e^(2πik/N)=1−4r sin²(πk/N), an independent spectral check. Finally Taylor expansion yields [u(t+Δt)−u(t)]/Δt=u_t+O(Δt), and [u(x+Δx)−2u(x)+u(x−Δx)]/Δx²=u_xx+O(Δx²). The heat equation cancels the leading terms. In the stable range, summing the resulting one-step defects gives a global fixed-time error of the same order under the stated smoothness in the normalized grid norm, with a uniform bound on the sampled consistency defect. A reaction term or boundary update changes these steps and must be analyzed separately.

title: Regular-singular equations, normalized bases and monodromy
central_question: How should a parameter-dependent local basis be chosen so logarithms, resonances and continuation data remain meaningful?
synopsis: Frobenius and Picard–Fuchs questions recur in scalar connections, elliptic periods, gauge changes and Hill equations. A differential equation is not determined by an evocative period name: its coefficients, singularities, normalization and initial or cycle data must be supplied. Once the operator is known, coefficient recurrence and a Wronskian provide concrete local information. When exponents collide, a raw basis can appear singular even if the solution space varies regularly. The divided-difference model below makes the logarithm appear explicitly and proves which pole is removable. It also exhibits nontrivial unipotent monodromy with eigenvalues equal to one, explaining why those eigenvalues do not imply trivial continuation. General Fuchsian systems require additional resonance compatibility conditions; the model is a constructive baseline rather than a replacement for the missing operator.
definitions_json: ["For t>0 let θ=t d/dt and L_ε=θ(θ+ε). Its indicial exponents are 0 and −ε.","For ε≠0 define g_ε(t)=(t^(−ε)−1)/ε. A branch of log t must be fixed for complex continuation.","A fundamental pair of scalar solutions has nonzero Wronskian. Monodromy records how a chosen basis changes after analytic continuation around a singular point."]
theorem_statement: g_ε extends analytically in ε to g₀=−log t. The pair (1,g_ε) remains independent with Wronskian −t^(−ε−1). Writing g_ε=Σ_{r≥0}ε^r g_r yields g_r=(−1)^(r+1)(log t)^(r+1)/(r+1)!, θ²g₀=0 and θ²g_r=−θg_(r−1) for r≥1.
theorem_proof: Choose a simply connected punctured domain and one analytic logarithm. Then t^(−ε)=exp(−ε log t) is entire in ε for each fixed t. Its exponential Taylor expansion shows that the numerator vanishes to first order at ε=0, so division removes the apparent pole and gives the stated coefficients. Both 1 and t^(−ε) solve L_εf=0, hence so does their divided difference. Direct differentiation gives g_ε′=−t^(−ε−1), never zero on the chosen domain; the Wronskian therefore has a finite nonzero limit −1/t. This proves independence even when the original pair (1,t^(−ε)) coalesces. Substituting the ε-series into (θ²+εθ)g=0 and equating coefficients gives the triangular hierarchy. It can also be checked directly using θ(log t)^k=k(log t)^(k−1). After a positive loop around zero, log t gains 2πi, so the limiting second solution −log t gains −2πi times the first. In the basis (1,−log t), continuation is represented by a nonidentity unipotent matrix, although both of its eigenvalues are one. The construction distinguishes a removable basis pole from genuine singular boundary data. For an actual Picard–Fuchs operator, its Frobenius recurrence and resonance equations must still be derived from that operator, rather than imported from this Euler example.

title: Asymptotic expansions, singular scales and exponentially small data
central_question: What does a finite asymptotic expansion determine, and how can its remainder and missing exponential contribution be made explicit?
synopsis: The asymptotic strand includes renormalization flows, spectral gaps, elliptic logarithms, cubic folds, Mathieu perturbation, and a factorial Borel model. Its common requirement is to state the small parameter, the approach sector and the uniformity of a remainder. A formal series can be useful while diverging everywhere; convergence and asymptotic accuracy are distinct. Conversely, a few perturbative coefficients cannot determine a global continuation, a Stokes constant or a nonlinear front law. The one-pole Borel example makes the distinction fully constructive. Its coefficients, exact integral, finite error bound and exponentially small solution ambiguity are all explicit. The cubic fold supplies a complementary algebraic scale: coalescing critical points produce a three-halves action difference and a two-thirds transition parameter. Each model has its own hypotheses and should not be promoted to a universal description by analogy.
definitions_json: ["The formal series F(z)=Σ_{n≥0}n!z^(n+1) has zero radius of convergence. Its Borel transform is B(t)=Σt^n=1/(1−t) near t=0.","For a>0 define the nonsingular negative-ray sum F(−a)=−∫₀∞e^(−u/a)/(1+u)du.","An asymptotic expansion controls the error after each fixed finite truncation as a parameter tends to a limit; it need not converge when infinitely many terms are added."]
theorem_statement: For every a>0 and N≥1, |F(−a)−Σ_{n=0}^{N−1}n!(−a)^(n+1)|≤N!a^(N+1). The corresponding Laplace sums solve z²F′−F=−z. Any two solutions differ by Ce^(−1/z); with above-minus-below bypasses of the positive Borel pole, the lateral difference is 2πi e^(−1/z).
theorem_proof: The exact finite geometric identity gives 1/(1+u)=Σ_{n=0}^{N−1}(−u)^n+(−u)^N/(1+u). Integrate against −e^(−u/a). The nth term evaluates to (−1)^(n+1)n!a^(n+1) by the Mellin moment. The absolute remainder is bounded by ∫₀∞e^(−u/a)u^Ndu=N!a^(N+1), since 1/(1+u)≤1. This proves a genuine finite-order error estimate on the negative ray even though the coefficient ratio makes the infinite power series divergent for every nonzero argument. Differentiation under the convergent integral, or integration by parts in its Laplace form, gives the inhomogeneous equation. Subtracting two solutions gives H′=H/z², hence H=Ce^(−1/z), which is smaller than every power as z↓0 on the positive ray. To compare the two lateral integrals, their difference closes clockwise around t=1. The residue of e^(−t/z)/(1−t) is −e^(−1/z), giving +2πi e^(−1/z) in that convention. The exponential ambiguity is therefore visible without guessing it from several factorial coefficients. A complete sectorial asymptotic proof must keep the bypass and decay contour fixed in a compatible sector; the explicit negative-ray bound is the directly verified remainder used here.

title: Stability in the right metric, including transient and hybrid behavior
central_question: Which norm or storage function certifies decay when eigenvalues, Euclidean growth and switching tell different stories?
synopsis: The stability strand is unusually consistent across the years: feedback can be asymptotically stable and still amplify an initial perturbation, a spectral gap depends on the modes actually observed, and changing metrics can reveal coercivity absent in the Euclidean symmetric part. A positive quadratic Lyapunov function supplies a constructive certificate. Its matrix also quantifies the cost of a coordinate change, forcing, switching and resets. These are capabilities with distinct inputs: an eigenvalue calculation, a transient-gain calculation and a hybrid dwell-time bound are related but answer different questions. The two-dimensional triangular model below is deliberately small enough to solve exactly. It proves decay in one metric while displaying temporary growth in another, giving a positive explanation for the archive’s repeated cautions about nonnormality.

It implies ||e^(tA)x||_P≤e^(−αt)||x||_P.","For hybrid switching, a metric jump ratio ρ≥1 bounds V_after≤ρV_before; an average dwell-time bound controls how often this cost can be incurred."]
theorem_statement: For A=[[-1,3],[0,−1]] and P=[[1/2,3/4],[3/4,11/4]], P>0 and AᵀP+PA=−I. Since P≤3I, ||e^(tA)x||_P≤e^(−t/6)||x||_P. Nevertheless the Euclidean squared norm has positive derivative at x=(1,1).
theorem_proof: The leading principal entry of P is 1/2 and det P=11/8−9/16=13/16>0, so the two-by-two Sylvester criterion proves positive definiteness. Direct multiplication gives AᵀP+PA=−I. Along x′=Ax, V′=xᵀ(AᵀP+PA)x=−||x||₂². The matrix 3I−P has positive first entry 5/2 and determinant (5/2)(1/4)−9/16=1/16>0, so P≤3I. Therefore ||x||₂²≥V/3 and V′≤−V/3. Integration and square roots give the rate 1/6 in the P norm. In contrast, at x=(1,1), Ax=(2,−1), so d||x||₂²/dt=2xᵀAx=2>0. The eigenvalues of A are both −1; their location does not prohibit this initial Euclidean amplification. Because A=−I+3N with N²=0, its exact exponential is e^(−t)(I+3tN), explicitly displaying the polynomial transient. If continuous segments obey V′≤−2αV and jumps cost at most ρ, then V(t)≤ρ^N(t)e^(−2αt)V(0). Under N(t)≤N₀+t/τ, this becomes ρ^N₀ exp[−2(α−logρ/(2τ))t]V(0). Thus switching consumes a precise logarithmic decay budget rather than preserving stability merely because each mode is stable.

title: Local bifurcation, exact cycles and the boundary of chaos claims
central_question: Which changes of stability can be derived from a return map, and what additional work separates a local bifurcation from global chaos?
synopsis: The dynamics archive repeatedly returns to logistic period doubling, oscillator locking, pitchfork regulation, scalar flip equations and return-map jets. These are best organized around a local map or flow, its invariant branches and its multipliers. A nonlinearity is not itself chaos, a symbolic analogy is not a conjugacy, and a local germ is not a global attractor. The logistic family offers an unusually complete positive example: the first fixed-point instability, the born two-cycle and its entire linear-stability interval follow from exact algebra. Later 2026 questions enrich this with explicit transcendental flip candidates, square-root branching and cubic coefficients of the second iterate. Those mechanisms can be compared once the local coordinates and nondegeneracy conditions are stated.

theorem_statement: The nonzero logistic fixed point is stable for 1<r<3. For r>3 its genuine two-cycle has points x_±=[r+1±√((r−3)(r+1))]/(2r) and multiplier m₂=−r²+2r+4. It is linearly attracting exactly for 3<r<1+√6.
theorem_proof: Solving f_r(x)=x gives zero and x*=1−1/r. At x*, f_r′(x*)=r(1−2+2/r)=2−r, whose absolute value is less than one exactly when 1<r<3. To locate period-two points, expand f_r²(x)−x and divide by the known fixed-point factors. The remaining equation is r²x²−r(r+1)x+(r+1)=0. Its discriminant is r²(r−3)(r+1), giving the displayed distinct real roots for r>3. Their sum is (r+1)/r and product is (r+1)/r². Consequently f_r′(x_+)f_r′(x_-)=r²[1−2(x_++x_-)+4x_+x_-]=−r²+2r+4. For r>3 this polynomial decreases strictly, starts at +1 at r=3 and reaches −1 at r=1+√6. Hence |m₂|<1 precisely on the stated interval. At the first endpoint the two-cycle merges with the fixed branch; at the second, its multiplier reaches the next flip boundary. This calculation establishes neither every later doubling nor Feigenbaum universality. A complementary jet calculation explains why higher terms matter: if R(s)=−s+as²+bs³+O(s⁴), direct composition gives R²(s)=s−2(a²+b)s³+O(s⁴); the quadratic term cancels and the sign or vanishing of a²+b is relevant. A multiplier of −1 alone omits that information.

title: Mechanics, dimensional modeling and invariant flow coordinates
central_question: Which quantities and scaling laws survive a change of coordinates, units or time parameter?
synopsis: The modeling strand includes mechanics, population and asset recurrences, conductance gates, mass balances and renormalization flows. Its common discipline is to identify state variables, units, conserved quantities and the meaning of the time parameter before interpreting a formula. Dimensional consistency narrows possible equations but does not determine numerical coefficients, boundary conditions or a physical mechanism. Hamiltonian mechanics supplies a precise constructive invariant: energy conservation. A simple turning point then exhibits two different exponents for physical time and abbreviated action. Their difference is caused by the measure being integrated, not a contradiction. The RG examples use the same chain-rule discipline to distinguish an invariant linearization exponent from coordinate-dependent higher coefficients. These are typed bridges between calculations, rather than a claim that every model in the family describes the same physics.

The meaning of the time variable remains part of this definition."]
theorem_statement: For the stated Hamiltonian, H is conserved. If V(q)=E−F(q*−q) exactly on q≤q*, then with δ=q*−q the remaining travel time is T(δ)=√(2/F)δ^(1/2), while the action length is S(δ)=(2/3)√(2F)δ^(3/2). At any scalar-flow fixed point, dβ_h/dh=β′(g*) under a smooth invertible state-coordinate change.
theorem_proof: Energy conservation is a direct chain-rule calculation: H′=V′(q)q′+pp′=V′p−pV′=0. On the increasing branch p=√[2(E−V(q))]=√(2Fδ). Physical travel time integrates dq/p, so T(δ)=∫₀^δ(2Fs)^(−1/2)ds=√(2/F)√δ. The abbreviated action integrates p dq, giving S(δ)=∫₀^δ√(2Fs)ds=(2/3)√(2F)δ^(3/2). The two powers therefore concern different observables. For a smooth potential with a nonzero turning derivative, Taylor’s theorem produces these leading terms with controlled local remainders; a degenerate turning point has different exponents. For the scalar coordinate calculation, differentiate β_h=φ′β with respect to h using d/dh=(φ′)^(−1)d/dg. The result is β′+(φ″/φ′)β. At a fixed point β(g*)=0, the second term vanishes and the linearized exponent is unchanged. This conclusion uses a state-coordinate change with φ′ nonzero and the same time. A rescaling of time multiplies the rate and must not be silently included. Exact flow integration makes the same point: for g′=bg², 1/g(t)=1/g₀−bt on every interval avoiding its pole. The finite-time wall is a property of that stated flow, not a physically meaningful singularity without an identified scale convention.

title: Memory, recurrence and the information needed for a closed evolution
central_question: When does a reduced state determine its own future, and what exact memory or symbolic data repair a failure of closure?
synopsis: A final dynamics strand connects hidden-variable elimination, damped recurrences, rotations, substitutions, cellular automata and path-dependent accumulators. The shared question is what information must be retained for a well-defined next state. Eliminating a hidden coordinate usually creates a memory kernel and an initial-state source. Forgetting either can turn an exact reduction into a different equation. Symbolic models pose the discrete analogue: an observed label may not encode the phase or history needed for the future. At the same time, deterministic aperiodicity can be highly structured. A rotation coding has exact balance, and a dense quasiperiodic orbit can have zero entropy. The family therefore organizes recurrence by a declared state, observation and equivalence relation rather than grouping every irregular-looking sequence under chaos.

A closed scalar evolution in x alone must determine x′ from retained data.","The memory convolution (K*x)(t)=∫₀ᵗK(t−s)x(s)ds retains past x values. The source be^(−dt)y₀ carries the hidden initial condition.","A mechanical word is w_n=⌊(n+1)α+ρ⌋−⌊nα+ρ⌋ for 0<α<1. It codes a rotation with an explicitly retained phase."]
theorem_statement: Eliminating y gives exactly x′(t)=−ax(t)+be^(−dt)y₀+bc∫₀ᵗe^(−d(t−s))x(s)ds. For a=d=b=c=1 and (x₀,y₀)=(1,0), x(t)=(1+e^(−2t))/2. Moreover every length-m block of the mechanical word has either ⌊mα⌋ or ⌈mα⌉ ones.
theorem_proof: Multiply the y-equation by e^(dt). Its derivative is c e^(dt)x(t); integrate from zero to t and divide by e^(dt) to obtain y(t)=e^(−dt)y₀+c∫₀ᵗe^(−d(t−s))x(s)ds. Substitution into the x-equation proves the exact Volterra equation and shows why the initial source cannot be omitted. In the stated symmetric example, s=x+y satisfies s′=0 and r=x−y satisfies r′=−2r. With s₀=r₀=1, x=(s+r)/2=(1+e^(−2t))/2 and y=(1−e^(−2t))/2. Dropping the memory would give e^(−t), which has the wrong long-time limit. This is an exact closure failure, not an approximation estimate. For the mechanical word, sum from n=j to j+m−1: the floors telescope to ⌊(j+m)α+ρ⌋−⌊jα+ρ⌋. Writing jα+ρ as integer plus θ∈[0,1) gives ⌊mα+θ⌋, which is either floor or ceiling of mα. Any two length-m blocks therefore differ in their number of ones by at most one. Dividing the prefix count by m yields limiting frequency α. If α is irrational, a periodic binary word would have rational frequency, so the word is aperiodic. These two examples demonstrate distinct constructive repairs: keep a memory term for the continuous reduction, or keep the rotation phase for the symbolic coding. Neither irregular recurrence nor aperiodicity alone proves positive entropy or unpredictability.

title: Probability laws, moments and joint dependence
central_question: Which parts of a conclusion follow from marginal probabilities, and which require a full joint law?
synopsis: A probability model is an assignment of mass to compatible outcomes before it is a formula for an average. The earliest finite probability questions, the distinction between population and amplitude weights, reliability calculations, Bayesian prediction and the final three-item surplus model all converge on this point. Linearity of expectation survives dependence, whereas the probability of a conjunction generally does not. The most productive revision is to preserve the entire compatibility structure until the requested functional has been calculated. A mean, a variance, a tail probability and an optimal action use different parts of that structure. This family therefore treats uncertainty as a mathematical input with explicitly stated moments, rather than as a single decorative error bar.

Thus independence conditional on one variable cannot be silently transported through marginalization. The proof also identifies the missing datum: a coupling or a latent-parameter distribution.

A random complex cannot be understood solely by calling it random: its vertex law, face rule, dependence and filtration parameter must be declared. Once those inputs are fixed, indicator expansion often turns a seemingly global expected invariant into a short exact sum. This family organizes three scales of the same idea: finite subset enumeration, order statistics of random birth times, and weak approximation of measures by coupled partial constructions.

title: Stochastic dynamics, Itô correction and finite-horizon prediction
central_question: Which drift, noise and observation model determines the uncertainty at a future time?
synopsis: The stochastic strand becomes coherent when a process is specified before its spectrum, stationary law or prediction error is computed. Finite reversible chains, a two-spin Gibbs model, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics, bridge functionals and exact linear propagation supply complementary levels of resolution. The key unification is the generator: transition rates in a finite state space and second derivatives in a diffusion both encode how expectations evolve. They do not make deterministic gradient descent, white noise and colored fluctuations interchangeable. The prediction problem adds a second layer: an observation changes the present conditional law, then a common transition propagates that law and introduces fresh process noise. Reversibility supplies a complementary finite certificate: detailed balance makes a Markov generator symmetric after weighting by its stationary law, so its relaxation modes can be checked spectrally. That self-adjoint reduction is specific to the declared chain and is not available for arbitrary driven dynamics.

title: Scaling limits, stable laws and the geometry of approximation
central_question: When does repeated averaging simplify a law, and which quantitative information survives the limit?
synopsis: Averaging, renormalization, heavy tails, multiplicative products and infinite-dimensional Gaussian models share a demand for explicit scaling. A Gaussian fixed point is a theorem about normalized sums with finite variance, not a universal fate of every noise source. Cauchy stability provides an exact countermodel, and multiplicative products become additive only after taking logarithms. The fractal measure construction adds a different kind of approximation: convergence follows from a direct coupling bound rather than from a central limit theorem. This family distinguishes exact finite identities, limiting distributions and numerical approximations, preserving the assumptions that make each useful.

theorem_statement: If a centered nondegenerate finite-variance law is fixed under R_α, then α=2; under R_2 its characteristic function is Gaussian. More generally R^k(X) converges in distribution to the centered Gaussian of variance v when EX=0 and EX²=v<∞.
theorem_proof: A fixed law has v=2·2^{−2/α}v, so nonzero finite v forces α=2. In that case the characteristic-function equation implies φ(t)=[φ(t/√n)]^n for dyadic n. Finite variance and centering give φ(s)=1−vs²/2+o(s²). Inserting s=t/√n and letting n grow yields exp(−vt²/2), proving the fixed-law assertion. The same expansion applied to the normalized sum of n independent copies proves convergence of characteristic functions, and hence convergence in distribution, for dyadic n and for the usual all-n central limit theorem. If higher cumulants exist, the rth cumulant scales as n^{1−r/2}; this records the disappearance of finite higher-order cumulants without asserting a uniform density approximation or a rate from only two moments.

title: Covariance geometry, nonlinear uncertainty and hidden-target risk
central_question: Which uncertainty is reducible by precision, and which requires a different observation?
synopsis: The covariance strand connects finite quadratic forms, data fusion, singular maps and statistical observability. Its central revision is to separate an exact law from a linearized uncertainty approximation, and to separate noise in an observed coordinate from a target component that the observation never determines. Positive semidefiniteness is a structural constraint on covariances, not merely a numerical preference. The observation sigma-algebra determines what can be estimated; the loss determines what error means. Together these ideas give a precise route from a hidden coordinate to an irreducible risk, while preventing a zero Jacobian from being read as zero nonlinear uncertainty.

title: Entropy contraction, channel information and Fisher geometry
central_question: Which information quantity is monotone under a declared transformation, and what geometry does it induce?
synopsis: Entropy appears across finite chains, communication channels, softmax models, quantum states and gradient diffusion. The synthesis needs a reference measure and a transformation before it needs a slogan about disorder. Shannon entropy can decrease under a nonuniform Markov equilibrium while relative entropy to that equilibrium decreases as well. central_question: Which feasible set and objective make a proposed improvement mathematically meaningful?
synopsis: Many optimization questions initially hide their most consequential choice: what is being optimized over which alternatives. title: Shared uncertainty, robust margins and decision-sufficient measurement
central_question: What must be measured to certify the decision, rather than reconstruct every uncertain score?
synopsis: The final decision strand ties the archive together especially well. Earlier finite thresholds, singular covariance optimization, normalized residual margins and later target-observation questions lead to a precise endpoint: compare the competing actions under the same compatible state. Independent score intervals can erase cancellation and make an easy decision look unresolved. A decision difference may depend on only a small part of a high-dimensional uncertainty set. The best experiment can therefore be one that resolves the sign of that difference, even if it leaves most of the system unknown. This is a mathematical design principle with deterministic quantifiers, distinct from a posterior preference or an empirical forecast.

title: Exact populations: products, recurrences and reversible addresses
central_question: How can a finite combinatorial population be counted, optimized and indexed without confusing objects with their statistics?
synopsis: The recurring constructive idea is to make an object contribute exactly once to a finite sum. A partition contributes a monomial through its part multiplicities; a tableau contributes through the position of its largest entry; a project selection contributes through one factor for every labeled project. These constructions give independent descriptions of the same population rather than a fit to its reported size. They also explain why equal weights do not merge labeled selections and why a terminal in a reduced decision diagram can represent many assignments. Once completion counts are available, enumeration becomes an address system: the same integers support counting, conditional queries, exact uniform sampling, and an optimum proved by a threshold population of size one. The mathematical advance is the unification of these operations under a single disjoint decomposition. It does not require trusting an optimizer or assuming that a compact diagram has already retained every multiplicity.

theorem_statement: For nonnegative weights, C(i,b)=C(i+1,b)+C(i+1,b−w_i), with C(i,b)=0 if a capacity coordinate is negative and C(n,b)=1 otherwise. These counts yield inverse bijections rank:Ω→{0,…,|Ω|−1} and unrank. A feasible object of profit v is the unique maximizer if the count of feasible objects with profit at least v equals one.
theorem_proof: Split each population according to its next bit. The two pieces are disjoint and correspond exactly to the smaller residual capacities, proving the recurrence by induction. If the entire suffix fits, every remaining bit is free and contributes 2^{n−i}; an omitted block of g coordinates therefore contributes a factor 2^g. In lexicographic order the zero branch occupies an initial address interval of length C(q0); the one branch occupies the next interval. Unranking compares an address with C(q0), subtracting that count in the one branch; ranking performs the inverse additions. Induction down the tree proves a bijection, including empty branches. A uniform address consequently induces a uniform object. Finally a singleton threshold population includes the supplied feasible witness, excludes every higher-profit object and excludes every competing equal-profit object. This proves optimum and uniqueness together.

title: Graph observations: spectra, cut censuses and stronger energy probes
central_question: Which graph features survive an observation, and what extra measurement separates a known collision?
synopsis: The graph thread develops from a warning about incomplete spectral observations into an exact hierarchy of finite invariants. A graph can be encoded by its adjacency matrix, its Laplacian, a heat operator, a heat trace, diagonal heat signatures, binary cut statistics or integer-height energy coefficients. These are different observation maps. Equality at one level need not imply equality at a richer level, and a numerical agreement at several parameters does not prove equality of a polynomial invariant. The productive method is to construct a full exact collision, identify the discarded correlations, then design a stronger finite observation. Incidence identities provide a parallel constructive route: singular values of a point-line incidence matrix determine the spectrum of its bipartite Levi graph. The centered Green matrix adds a variational capacity, translating a graph operator into an exact energy required to force one coordinate while maintaining zero mean.

title: Incidence kernels, path differences and primal–dual graph witnesses
central_question: How do local incidence constraints produce global cycles, and when does a short witness prove an optimal graph action count?
synopsis: Incidence is the common finite language for conservation, cycle spaces, graph gauge classes and many covering arguments. An oriented edge is sent to the difference of its endpoint vertices; cancellation at internal vertices explains why a path has only source and sink boundary. Subtracting two paths therefore produces a circulation. The converse requires hypotheses: in a finite source-to-sink directed acyclic graph with every edge covered by a path, these differences span the entire real circulation space. Acyclic direction does not erase undirected cycles; a diamond already has a one-dimensional incidence kernel. The complementary optimization theme is that an admissible construction establishes an upper bound, while a matching or other dual witness establishes a lower bound. A support size or observed action count has no optimality meaning until the permitted action is stated. This family makes that action model and its certificate visible.

A matching consists of edges with disjoint endpoints, so any one vertex-call covers at most one matching edge.","For a graph regarded as a one-dimensional complex, H_1=ker B because there are no two-cells. Adding filled faces changes the quotient by their boundaries."]
theorem_statement: The incidence rank is n−c, hence the circulation dimension is m−n+c. On a finite directed acyclic s-to-t graph with every edge on an s-to-t path, ker B is spanned over R by χ(p)−χ(p₀). In the vertex-call model on K_{a,b}, the exact minimum call count is min(a,b).
theorem_proof: On each connected component, incidence columns sum to zero and hence rank is at most n_component−1. A spanning tree contributes independent columns: remove a leaf and inspect its unique incident coefficient, inductively forcing every coefficient to zero. Summing components proves the rank formula. Every path difference has zero boundary. For the converse sum covering path indicators to obtain a strictly positive feasible flow f. For z∈ker B, both f and f+εz are nonnegative for small enough ε. A finite DAG permits a decomposition of each into nonnegative s-to-t path flows: follow positive flow, use conservation internally, and subtract the least path-edge value. At least one edge is removed at each stage. Their source divergence is the same, so subtracting the decompositions gives a combination of path differences. Finally assume a≤b. An a-edge matching demands at least a vertex-calls, and all a left vertices cover every edge. Matching lower bound and cover upper bound meet.

title: Separators, semiring elimination and multiplicity-preserving quotients
central_question: What boundary state is sufficient to compose local computations without changing a count or optimum?
synopsis: A large combinatorial computation is often tractable because a separator carries only the information that the unprocessed part can still observe. The mathematics is distributivity plus a correct boundary state, rather than a promise that every graph is sparse. Sum–product elimination computes counts or partition sums; min–plus elimination computes minimum additive costs. Both depend on the same factor scopes, but they answer different questions and require different identities. An auxiliary gate with a unique extension preserves the number of original objects; an arbitrary satisfiability-preserving encoding may not. A channel quotient is legitimate only if forgotten lane identities cannot affect future feasibility or cost. These are not independent implementation details: they specify the exact relation between a compact state and the population or value it represents. The useful design process proves a local elimination identity, proves the quotient lift condition and retains enough separator data to make every future continuation well defined.

Its adequacy is a statement about every compatible continuation.","For a relation F(x,a), the auxiliary fibre m(x)=#{a:F(x,a)} measures whether projecting auxiliaries preserves a count."]
theorem_statement: Finite semiring elimination preserves Z by distributivity, in any elimination order. Over counting integers, an encoding preserves #P exactly when its satisfying auxiliary fibre is one over each x∈P and zero otherwise. If a quotient map is surjective onto feasible quotient states and feasibility and objective are constant on its fibres, the original and quotient optimum values are equal.
theorem_proof: Separate the factors involving v from the others. The independent factors can be taken outside ⊕_v, and the remaining expression is g by definition. Repetition proves exact elimination; changing order changes intermediate scopes but not the final algebraic value. Over integers, the number of satisfying pairs is Σ_x m(x), so unique extension gives #F=#P; mere existential equivalence does not control m(x). For optimization, every original object projects to a quotient object with equal cost, so the quotient infimum is no larger. Every feasible quotient object has a feasible lift with that cost, proving the reverse inequality. Future operations descend only when they preserve fibres as well, which is a stronger requirement than preserving the present objective.

title: Future equivalence, bisimulation and executable quotient states
central_question: When can two internal states be merged while preserving every permitted future observation?
synopsis: The correct state of a computation is relative to its observer and action alphabet. Two memories that currently print the same value may behave differently after a tick, reset, allocation or later query. Future equivalence compares every such continuation. In a finite deterministic machine, its apparently infinite definition has a finite certificate: iterative partition refinement stops at a stable partition, and stability implies agreement for every word. Weighted futures require immediate costs as well as visible outputs to descend. Bisimulation supplies a useful transition-level proof principle but must be stated for the actual operational semantics. The resulting quotient is an executable machine, not merely a partition of a log. This family is the central bridge between semantic state reduction, target-relative observations and efficient separator states. It explains both why some reductions are exact and why a dramatic reduction in state count alone establishes no behavioral equivalence.

A word acts in its given order.","Future equivalence is s∼t iff o(δ_w(s))=o(δ_w(t)) for every finite word w, including the empty word.","Depth-r equivalence checks words of length at most r. Refinement maps a state to its present output together with the current classes of all its successors.","With additive action costs, C_s(aw)=c(s,a)+C_{δ_a(s)}(w). A cost-preserving quotient must preserve these immediate costs and all successor classes."]
theorem_statement: Future equivalence is the coarsest equivalence respecting outputs and every action transition. Finite partition refinement computes it and has at most |S|−1 strict refinements. Once two successive partitions agree, the stable partition checks all word lengths. Equality of all accumulated continuation costs similarly defines a right congruence for deterministic weighted machines.
theorem_proof: If s and t have equal futures, then their present outputs agree. For every action a and every word w, the output after aw agrees; hence δ_a(s)∼δ_a(t), making the quotient transition independent of representatives. Conversely, any output-preserving transition congruence preserves the output after every word by induction, so it refines future equivalence. Starting from output classes, the next refinement checks exactly one more leading action by the same induction. A stable partition therefore preserves transitions and already equals the full relation. Every strict refinement increases the number of nonempty blocks, giving the finite bound. For additive costs, compare one-letter words first to obtain c(s,a)=c(t,a), then subtract this finite common value from the equality for aw to obtain future equality at the successors. This subtraction argument needs finite deterministic costs; nondeterministic min–plus machines require their own semantics.

title: Hankel witnesses and minimal observable memory
central_question: How can an exact realization and an independent lower bound prove the smallest recurrence or register dimension?
synopsis: State reduction has two logically different tasks. A proposed smaller machine must reproduce every output, and every still smaller machine must be ruled out within a declared encoding class. For linear systems these tasks meet through intertwiners and Hankel rank. A matrix identity transports the entire dynamics, while a nonzero finite minor prevents a lower-dimensional realization. This is stronger than fitting a recurrence to a prefix and more informative than quoting the dimension of the original state. Reachable and observable modes must be considered jointly: the zero-initial input-output order lives on the reachable space modulo its invisible part. A scalar universal output recurrence differs from a recurrence for one initial state, and multiple-output recurrence degree need not equal state dimension. In the min–plus setting a two-by-two response table provides a separate additive-register obstruction; ordinary field rank must not be imported into that semiring without justification.

The minimal zero-initial driven state is R/(R∩N).","A finite min–plus rank-one table has entries M_{ij}=u_i+v_j. Such a table has equal diagonal and off-diagonal sums on every two-by-two submatrix."]
theorem_statement: An r-state linear realization has Hankel rank at most r. An order-r forward recurrence has the same rank bound. Therefore an r-state realization together with a nonzero r-by-r Hankel minor proves exact minimal state dimension and recurrence order r. For scalar universal outputs on an observable quotient, the universal recurrence is the quotient operator’s minimal polynomial; its degree equals that observable quotient dimension.
theorem_proof: The intertwiner identity gives RA^n=G^nR by induction, and the input/output identities yield equality of every sequence term. Any finite Hankel block factors as rows cA^i times columns A^jb through the realization state space, so its rank cannot exceed the state dimension. A recurrence of order s expresses every later Hankel column as a fixed combination of the preceding s, giving the same lower bound. Conversely Cayley–Hamilton supplies a recurrence of order at most r for an r-state realization. For universal observation recurrences, N is A-invariant because CA^k(Av)=CA^{k+1}v. A polynomial p annihilates every future output exactly when p(A)V⊆N, or p(A_bar)=0. In the scalar observable case a lower-degree polynomial would make all observation rows dependent on fewer initial rows, contradicting observability.

title: Typed proof certificates and the boundary between examples and completeness
central_question: What exact claim does each certificate establish, and which dependencies remain outside its proof boundary?
synopsis: The archive repeatedly reaches the same useful discipline from different directions: separate a search procedure from a small exact checker, and state the checker’s theorem with its quantifiers and input type. A feasible point proves existence; a primal–dual equality proves optimality; a rank minor plus factorization proves rank; a Bézout identity proves inconsistency; a complete Gröbner replay proves an ideal basis. These witnesses are not interchangeable. Nor does checking many examples establish a universal identity unless a degree bound or other completeness theorem reduces the universal statement to those examples. This family turns that discipline into a reusable proof interface. It begins with truth tables and bound variables, continues through arithmetic and floating-point envelopes, and reaches exact algebraic and finite-state certificates. The goal is constructive: make a solver’s useful discoveries portable across a trust boundary while exposing the precise assumptions on which the conclusion rests.
definitions_json: ["A certificate is data c for an explicitly specified predicate Check(input,c). Soundness proves Check⇒Claim; completeness, if needed, proves every true claim has an admissible certificate.","A witness establishes ∃x P(x); a complete census establishes both listed⇒valid and valid⇒listed. These are distinct quantifier directions.","A polynomial over F_q reduced to degree below q in every variable is a different object from an arbitrary formal polynomial or a polynomial function modulo x_i^q−x_i.","A proof dependency record states the encoded instance, arithmetic domain, theorem hypotheses, checker implementation and any external mathematical theorem used."]
theorem_statement: If f∈F_q[x_1,…,x_n] has degree <q in each variable and vanishes on all q^n points, then f is the zero formal polynomial. Without this degree condition exhaustive functional agreement need not prove formal polynomial equality. Separately, exact primal and dual feasible points with equal objectives certify an LP optimum by weak duality.
theorem_proof: For the polynomial theorem, induct on n. A one-variable nonzero polynomial of degree <q cannot have q roots. Write f as a polynomial in the last variable. At every fixed earlier tuple all q evaluations vanish, so every coefficient evaluates to zero. Each coefficient retains the coordinate degree bounds, and induction makes all coefficient polynomials zero. Without the bound, x_1^q−x_1 vanishes everywhere but has nonzero coefficient dictionary. For LP minimization Ax=b,x≥0 and dual maximization bᵀy with Aᵀy≤c, every feasible pair satisfies bᵀy=yᵀAx≤cᵀx. Equality therefore sandwiches the optimum. title: Coding and raw-state recovery by exact lattice certificates
central_question: When do finitely many output words determine a hidden state, and how does that injectivity become optimal error correction?
synopsis: The coding thread begins with concrete binary codes whose distance can be independently enumerated and culminates in a universal certificate for a specified 107-bit raw generator. It is important to separate three achievements. Alphabet capacity gives a necessary observation count. A short-vector exclusion proves injectivity for every state, rather than only tested fixtures. Finally a distance argument converts injectivity of every five-position projection into optimal correction of corrupted words. The large proof has a compact trusted core: integer lattice membership, an exact determinant and rational inverse-column bounds. A basis reduction algorithm may discover useful matrices, but the checker does not trust that search. This makes the raw-state theorem a strong example of portable exact certification. The accepted-output sequence has hidden rejected steps and remains a different observation model; its earlier threshold claim cannot inherit the raw theorem.
definitions_json: ["Set M=2^107−1, A=3^121 mod M, b=2^26, x_{i+1}=Ax_i mod M and y_i=x_i mod b, with 0≤x_i<M.","For five known positions p_0<…<p_4 in {0,…,8}, let g_j=p_j−p_0 and Λ_p={d∈Z^5:d_j≡A^{g_j}d_0 mod M}. Set D=floor((M−1)/b)=2^81−1.","The raw trajectory code C_n consists of the first n output words of every state. Hamming distance counts changed words, even when many bits in a word are changed.","A supplied row basis B_p is certified by lattice row membership, |det B_p|=M^4, and DΣ_i|(B_p^{-1})_{ij}|<3/8 for every column j."]
theorem_statement: For every five-position subset of the first nine raw steps, the selected words uniquely determine the initial state. Four words cannot determine every state. For 5≤n≤9 the raw trajectory code has minimum distance exactly n−4. Thus seven words correct one arbitrary word error and nine correct two, and these lengths are optimal for any code representing all M states over this alphabet.
theorem_proof: The map d↦(d_j−A^{g_j}d_0)_{j=1}^4 onto (Z/MZ)^4 has kernel Λ_p, so the lattice index is M^4. Membership and matching determinant establish that the supplied rows span the whole lattice. If two states produce the same selected words, their selected state differences are bd_j with |d_j|≤D. Since b is invertible modulo M, d∈Λ_p, hence d=cB_p for integer c. The dual bound gives |c_j|≤DΣ_i|(B_p^{-1})_{ij}|<1, forcing c=0 and then equality of the initial states because A is invertible. Four words are impossible by b^4<M−1. Distinct length-n codewords agree in at most four positions, so d_min≥n−4. Puncturing d_min−1 positions is injective, giving M≤b^{n−d_min+1}; since M>b^4, d_min≤n−4. Disjoint radius-t Hamming balls require d_min>2t. Puncturing 2t positions then gives n≥5+2t, proving optimal lengths.

title: Target-relative observation: fibres, factorization and dynamic closure
central_question: Which hidden directions matter for the requested target, and when can the observation itself evolve as a closed state?
synopsis: The strongest common thread in the later archive is that full-state recovery is often unnecessary. An observation can leave a large invisible fibre while still determining a particular target exactly. The right question asks whether the target is constant on those fibres. In finite-dimensional linear algebra this becomes a kernel inclusion, a factorization and a sharp stability inequality. This also separates three levels frequently merged in informal discussions: present target identifiability, stable noisy recovery and closed predictive dynamics. Present factorization G=LH does not imply that Hx can predict its own future; closure requires the invisible space to be invariant under the state dynamics. In nonlinear models a derivative test is only local and can miss second-order target variation along a hidden fibre. These distinctions guide sensor design constructively: retain or measure directions that change the target, then verify the closure or robustness property actually required by the task.
definitions_json: ["For state x∈V, observation H:V→W and target G:V→Z, a fibre is {x:Hx=y}. The target is identifiable if Hx=Hx′ implies Gx=Gx′.","The invisible space of a linear observation is ker H. Target-relative observability is ker H⊆ker G, not necessarily ker H={0}.","For dynamics x′=Ax, observation closure means there is T with HA=TH. A moving observation B(t) closes when B′+BA=TB.","For Euclidean finite-dimensional spaces, the minimum-norm recovery on im H is L₀=GH†; its extension can vanish on the orthogonal complement of im H."]
theorem_statement: The following are equivalent: G is identifiable from H; ker H⊆ker G; G=LH for some linear L; and GᵀG≼λHᵀH for some finite λ≥0. The smallest such λ is the squared minimum recovery norm. Separately, HA=TH exists exactly when ker H is A-invariant.
theorem_proof: Identifiability applied to x∈ker H and x′=0 gives the kernel inclusion. Conversely, equal observations differ by a vector in ker H, so their targets agree. Define L(Hx)=Gx on im H; the inclusion makes this independent of the chosen representative and gives linearity. Extend L to W. Factorization gives ||Gx||≤||L||||Hx|| and hence the quadratic inequality. Conversely the inequality forces Gx=0 whenever Hx=0. The least possible norm is the supremum of ||Gx||/||Hx|| over nonzero observed vectors, exactly the least square-root constant in the inequality; the zero extension attains it in finite dimensions. For closure, HA must vanish on ker H, which is equivalent to A(ker H)⊆ker H. Apply the same factorization construction with target HA. In moving coordinates differentiate Bx and obtain (B′+BA)x; this is a new target to which the criterion applies.

The minimum recovery norm is √2 because H is onto R² and L=(1,1). Requesting x₁ instead fails: x and x+(1,−1,1) have the same observation and different first coordinates. For H(x,z)=x and nonlinear target g(x,z)=z², the hidden derivative ∂_z g vanishes at z=0, yet g changes along that same observation fibre. Thus a zero directional derivative at one point is not finite-amplitude identifiability. In periodic velocity reconstruction, divergence and curl similarly leave a constant harmonic mean invisible unless it is separately observed.","meaning":"A target can be recovered with fewer channels than a whole state, but stable recovery, future prediction and nonlinear global identifiability each need their own theorem."}

title: Control energies, compatible metrics and constrained descriptor dynamics
central_question: How can a declared system carry a complete stability, reachability or optimal-control certificate?
synopsis: Control claims become concrete only after the plant, allowed inputs, output and state domain are specified. A positive Lyapunov matrix proves decay in one chosen metric; stable eigenvalues alone need not make Euclidean energy decrease at every instant. Finite-horizon Gramians quantify reachability and observation without requiring asymptotic stability. Riccati equations certify quadratic control values through completion of squares, including the terminal condition. Descriptor systems add algebraic constraints: a singular mass matrix can encode a regular constrained evolution, and replacing it by an invertible approximation can introduce a wholly new unstable mode. The common constructive capacity is to certify the property of the actual model with exact matrix identities. It is not enough to import a gain, a condition number or a contraction claim from a nearby surrogate. Norm bounds and dynamics must refer to the same metric and the same invariant domain.

Consistent initial states must satisfy its algebraic constraints.","For scalar x′=u and cost ∫(x²+u²)dt, a value coefficient P solves a Riccati equation; the admissible horizon and terminal value are part of its definition."]
theorem_statement: If P≻0 and AᵀP+PA=−Q with Q≻0, then V(t)≤e^{−λ_min(Q)t/λ_max(P)}V(0). For any T>0, W_c(T)≻0 iff [B,AB,…,A^{n−1}B] has rank n; the analogous observation statement holds. For x′=u on [0,T] with zero terminal cost, P(t)=tanh(T−t) gives the optimal feedback u=−P(t)x and value P(0)x(0)².
theorem_proof: Differentiate V to get V′=−xᵀQx≤−[λ_min(Q)/λ_max(P)]V and integrate. For the Gramian, vᵀW_cv=∫||Bᵀe^{Aᵀt}v||²dt. It vanishes exactly when this analytic function is zero on the interval, equivalently Bᵀ(Aᵀ)^kv=0 for every k. Cayley–Hamilton reduces this to k<n, proving the rank equivalence and the dual observation result. For the Riccati model, P′=P²−1 and P(T)=0. Along any admissible control, x²+u²+d(Px²)/dt=(u+Px)². Integration gives cost=P(0)x(0)²+∫(u+Px)²dt because the terminal term vanishes. The proposed feedback makes the square zero and therefore attains the exact lower bound.

title: Regularized inverse problems: bias, noise and certified stopping
central_question: How should finite resolution be chosen when inversion amplifies measurement error?
synopsis: Inverse problems make a precise tradeoff visible: a richer inverse reduces approximation bias but amplifies noise. A source class says which signals are admissible; a deterministic noise ball says which data can be trusted. The archive’s strongest late analytic development derives matching upper and lower recovery rates for concrete diagonal models rather than asserting convergence from a suggestive cutoff formula. Mild singular-value decay gives a power-law rate, severe decay gives a logarithmic rate, and the latter requires a lower-order safety margin. Tikhonov and Landweber express the same controlled approximation through different spectral filters. The constructive payoff is a parameter or stopping rule with a declared worst-case bound. A rate is not just a fitted slope: an indistinguishable pair shows that no recovery map can uniformly do better on the stated signal class.
definitions_json: ["Observe y^δ=Ax+η in Hilbert norm with ||η||≤δ and x in a source class M. A linear reconstruction R has bias B_M(R)=sup_{x∈M}||(RA−I)x||.","For diagonal Ae_k=σ_ke_k, spectral cutoff R_N retains k≤N and divides those coordinates by σ_k.","Use the ellipsoid M_r={x:Σk^{2r}|x_k|²≤1}. Mild decay is σ_k=k^{−p}; severe decay is σ_k=e^{−ck^β}, with all parameters positive.","Tikhonov R_α=(A* A+αI)^{-1}A* and Landweber early stopping are bounded spectral filters approximating the unbounded inverse."]
theorem_statement: For any bounded R, the worst-case error is at most B_M(R)+δ||R||. Mild cutoff N=floor(δ^{−1/(p+r)}) has minimax order δ^{r/(p+r)}. Severe cutoff with L=log(1/δ) and N=floor(((L−(r/β)log L)/c)^{1/β}) has minimax order L^{−r/β} for sufficiently large L. Merely requiring N∼(L/c)^{1/β} does not guarantee convergence.
theorem_proof: Decompose Ry^δ−x=(RA−I)x+Rη and use the triangle inequality. On M_r the cutoff bias is (N+1)^{−r}; its noise norm is δ/σ_N. For polynomial singular values, balance N^{−r} with δN^p to obtain the power-law upper bound. Choose K of order δ^{−1/(p+r)} and x_±=±K^{−r}e_K. Both signals lie in the ellipsoid and have ||Ax_±||≤δ after a harmless integer adjustment, so the same datum zero is admissible for both. Any estimator must err by at least K^{−r} on one, proving the matching order. For severe decay, the stated safety margin gives δe^{cN^β}≤L^{−r/β} while N^{−r} has the same order. A K of order (L/c)^{1/β} gives the analogous two-point lower bound. But with c=β=1,δ=e^{−j},N=j, the leading asymptotic cutoff holds and noise amplification equals one; convergence fails.

For Landweber with 0<ω≤||A||^{-2}, m steps give bias ≤ρ(ν/(eωm))^ν and noise ≤δ√(ωm). More iterations can therefore worsen the total guarantee after the bias-noise balance.","meaning":"The admissible class, operator spectrum and noise model jointly determine useful resolution; a cutoff or iteration count has no universal meaning on its own."}

title: Cheapest distinguishing experiments and uncertainty-aware decisions
central_question: Which next observation resolves the target at minimum guaranteed cost, and when does additional data remain irrelevant?
synopsis: Observation and decision become a single constructive problem when the remaining states and available tests are finite and explicit. A test splits the current feasible set into outcome fibres. A target is resolved when it is constant on the surviving set, even if the full hidden state remains unknown. Positive test costs lead to an exact worst-case Bellman recurrence with matching lower and upper proofs. This is a rigorous version of choosing the cheapest distinguishing experiment, and it complements linear target-factorization: one asks which extra measurement destroys the harmful ambiguity. Correlated uncertainty adds a geometric version. An ellipsoid has exact target extrema, while a hidden-target conditional variance can remain positive even with noiseless recorded channels. More readings do not automatically remove uncertainty if they repeat the same direction or measure variables unrelated to the target’s hidden component. The archive’s decision examples become strongest when their uncertainty sets and terminal target criterion are stated together.

Its outcome fibre is S_{e,y}={s∈S:e(s)=y}.","A terminal set is one on which τ is constant. A useful test has every nonempty outcome fibre a proper subset of the current nonterminal set.","For correlated uncertainty E={μ+Σ^{1/2}z:||z||≤r}, Σ is positive definite and a linear target is aᵀx.","Worst-case decision cost, expected cost under a prior and statistical information gain are different objectives."]
theorem_statement: If the available tests separate every pair of states having different target values, the least worst-case cost is V(S)=0 on terminal sets and otherwise V(S)=min_e[c_e+max_{y:S_{e,y}≠∅}V(S_{e,y})], over useful tests. For the ellipsoid E, the exact linear-target range is aᵀμ±r√(aᵀΣa).
theorem_proof: Any decision tree chooses a first test e. An adversary can return the outcome whose remaining subtree has largest optimal cost, so every tree costs at least c_e+max_yV(S_{e,y}). Minimizing gives the lower bound. Conversely attach optimal subtrees to a minimizing test. Every nonempty fibre is smaller, so induction on |S| constructs a tree attaining that same value. Pairwise target separation guarantees that a nonterminal set has a splitting test; otherwise two different target values could never be distinguished. Positive cost lets us discard useless first tests. This proves existence and exact optimality. For the ellipsoid write aᵀx=aᵀμ+(Σ^{1/2}a)ᵀz. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the stated extrema, attained at z=±rΣ^{1/2}a/√(aᵀΣa) when a≠0. Correlation is retained through the quadratic form rather than discarded in independent coordinate bars.

title: Quantum states, coherence, channels and complete instruments
central_question: Which observations distinguish states, and which transformations preserve their physical probability structure?
synopsis:
The quantum information strand is best organised around a state, an observation map and an allowed transformation. A density matrix carries both populations and coherences; a measurement sees only selected linear functionals of that matrix. A channel must preserve positivity even when the system is coupled to an arbitrary ancilla, which is stronger than preserving trace or ordinary positivity. An instrument additionally records the classical measurement branch. These distinctions connect the early coherence example to later dephasing, error correction, leakage and sequential postselection discussions.

The Bell state and its fully dephased mixture are an especially clear organising pair. Computational-basis probabilities, diagonal parity and both one-qubit marginals agree exactly, while an off-diagonal correlation separates them. This is a complete finite instance of observation-relative identifiability, linking quantum tomography to the atlas-wide question of what a target can be reconstructed from. It does not imply that all measurements are blind; it identifies one observation algebra and an explicit additional observable that resolves its collision.

The transformation side is equally constructive. Kraus operators certify complete positivity by turning the channel tensored with any ancilla into a sum of positive conjugations. Their completeness equation certifies total probability. Dephasing changes only selected coherences, amplitude damping transfers populations and depolarisation contracts every traceless component. Error correction requires an actual error family: the three-qubit repetition code corrects single bit flips but has a weight-one logical phase error, hence quantum distance one. Sequential instruments force the success probability to remain visible through every branch. Normalizing a successful state is legitimate conditional probability, but cannot convert a rare success into an unconditional implementation guarantee.

title: Finite Weyl systems, symplectic Pauli geometry and projective phases
central_question: What finite operator relations can hold exactly, and how are their commutation and central phases certified?
synopsis:
Finite quantum algebra has a precise boundary. The canonical relation [Q,P]=iℏI cannot hold for finite matrices when ℏ≠0, because the trace of a commutator is zero. Clock and shift operators provide a consistent finite replacement, with multiplicative relation UV=qVU. Taking determinants forces q to be a root of unity, so a rational phase is an exact existence condition, whereas an irrational phase cannot have an exact finite invertible representation. Rational approximation changes the algebraic parameter; it does not remove this obstruction.

The finite models connect naturally to symplectic geometry. Pauli operators modulo scalar phase are labelled by binary vectors, and their commutation sign is an alternating bilinear form. Centralizers of a specified nonzero support become exact symplectic kernels. Sector transition counts are images of another pairing map and therefore require its actual kernel, not a superficially similar quotient. These finite linear maps are a constructive common core of symmetry reduction, stabilizer codes and operator selection rules.

Fourier and Gauss operators add projective phases. A quadratic refinement produces a symmetric polar form, while Pauli commutation uses an alternating form. At odd order these cannot be identified indiscriminately. The finite Weil relation (ST)³=γC records a Gauss phase γ that must be computed rather than normalized away without explanation. For the order-three example γ=i. This family therefore keeps three distinct certificates together: trace and determinant obstructions; exact finite operator bases; and central phases in group relations. It does not promote one finite matrix pair into categorical coherence or an infinite irrational rotation algebra.

title: Polynomial Moyal exactness and the complete bounded sextic monomial atlas
central_question: Exactly when does a polynomial Moyal bracket equal its Poisson bracket, and when does a vanished cubic correction hide a fifth-order defect?
synopsis:
The Moyal strand has a particularly strong cross-year synthesis because it begins with a formal product and ends with a finite coefficient classification. Fixing the Weyl convention makes every polynomial calculation exact. Antisymmetry removes the even bidifferential orders, while division by iℏ leaves only even powers ℏ^{k−1}. A different power convention cannot be mixed with these coefficients. For monomials, falling factorials turn differentiation into an integer formula; exactness is then the simultaneous vanishing of every active higher odd coefficient.

Two apparently conflicting source ideas become compatible after the degree bound is respected. The family (qp³,q^{3r+2}p^r) has vanishing cubic correction, and all fifth or higher derivatives of the first input vanish because its total degree is four. It is therefore an infinite exact family. Higher-degree pairs can genuinely hide a fifth-order obstruction. The pair (qp⁵,q⁵p³) gives a nonzero ℏ⁴ term despite S₃=0. The atlas adds a smaller witness entirely inside degree six and an exhaustive bounded monomial classification.

This added sextic result is a present synthesis, not a claim about what an earlier conversation proved. Among the twenty-eight monomials of total degree at most six, 504 of 784 ordered pairs are exact and 280 have a defect; four are invisible to the cubic test alone. Among the seven monomials of exactly degree six, fifteen of forty-nine ordered pairs are exact. These statements are complete for the declared finite monomial universe. Arbitrary linear combinations can cancel coefficients across different monomial pairs, so this enumeration is not a classification of all sextic polynomial pairs. At degree seven and above, S₇ and further terms become possible and must be retained.

The Poisson coefficient is r−3(3r+2)=−8r−6, proving the family uniformly rather than by sampling.

title: Braid representations, fusion rules and complete finite coherence data
central_question: Which explicit relations turn braid or fusion numbers into a consistent algebraic or categorical structure?
synopsis:
The braid and fusion discussions form a hierarchy of increasingly structured data. A braid representation requires matrices satisfying the braid relations. A Hecke relation imposes an additional quadratic quotient. A fusion ring records integer multiplication coefficients and a dimension homomorphism. A braided fusion category also requires associators and braidings satisfying pentagon and hexagon equations; a unitary realization requires positivity. A larger object count or a familiar exceptional dimension does not skip any of these stages.

Two finite models organise the hierarchy. The fundamental Hecke braid matrix provides a Laurent-polynomial Yang–Baxter calculation, with a simple rational specialization that is visibly nonunitary. The pointed four-object model supplies complete F,R,S data: labels add in F₂², the associator is one and a bilinear sign supplies the braiding. Every coherence equation reduces to a finite bilinearity identity, and character orthogonality gives modular nondegeneracy and Verlinde multiplication. This is a fully specified categorical example, whereas diagonalizing the Fibonacci fusion matrix alone certifies its ring data and dimensions but not every categorical coherence equation.

Temperley–Lieb provides a useful bridge between algebraic relations and positive quantum models. Rank-one projections satisfy the finite TL relations at a declared parameter; a trace then needs a separate positive Gram form. Already at two strands, |δ|<1 produces a negative value on x*x. Passing this small test does not prove positivity throughout an infinite tower. Similarly, a normalized bracket gives a conventioned trefoil Jones polynomial without becoming a complete knot invariant. The synthesis preserves these genuinely constructive models while making each change of mathematical type explicit.

title: Integrable models as finite spectral and tau-function bridges
central_question: How can an integrability claim be anchored simultaneously in an explicit operator and a verified scalar equation?
synopsis:
The integrable strand contains two complementary constructive bridges. A finite quantum spin chain can be diagonalized directly and compared with its Bethe parameterization. A classical nonlinear wave can be built from a tau-function whose bilinear identity fixes its interaction coefficient. In both cases a normalization connects descriptions that would otherwise remain a slogan. The bridge is useful because each side supplies an independent exact residual.

The four-site XXX chain has a one-magnon sector where the Hamiltonian becomes the cycle Laplacian. Fourier modes diagonalize it, and the finite regular Bethe roots reproduce all nonuniform modes. The uniform mode is present as an infinite-root limit, exposing why a list of finite roots need not be complete. The two-site Gaudin model offers a different spectral-to-differential bridge: a Bethe root supplies a singlet eigenvector and a Miura potential in which the apparent pole cancels exactly. The eigenvalues appear as residues at the physical marked points. This is a complete small calculation, rather than a proof of arbitrary Bethe completeness or a global automorphic correspondence.

The tau-function side similarly distinguishes interaction from superposition. For KdV, two independent one-soliton exponentials need a mixed exponential term, and its coefficient is forced by the Hirota polynomial. Positivity of the coefficients makes the real tau-function nonsingular. The same construction gives phase shifts and mass by asymptotics and boundary values of logτ. A y-independent solution embeds in the chosen KP equation, but transverse stability and general two-dimensional interactions are additional problems. The unifying capacity is not a universal solver: it is the ability to compare a finite spectral model, a scalar differential operator or a finite exponential identity under explicitly matched conventions.

title: Deformations, obstruction equations and Poisson transport
central_question: When does a first-order algebraic change extend to a genuine family, and which structural invariants can still jump?
synopsis:
Deformation is a family of equations, not an adjective attached to a new notation. Its data include a coefficient ring, an object, an equivalence relation and a compatibility equation at every order. In associative algebra, the first-order equation is a Hochschild cocycle condition. In a differential graded Lie model it becomes a Maurer–Cartan equation, with a second-order cohomology class measuring obstruction. Neither a tangent vector nor a long finite truncation proves an all-order extension without a theorem controlling the remaining equations.

Three small models make the distinctions explicit. A characteristic-two character of C₂ has a nontrivial tangent direction that cannot lift one order further. A dual-number multiplication can be deformed to x²=t as a free rank-two algebra, yet its positive-degree Hochschild cohomology jumps at the special fibre. A reflection-deformed derivative on polynomials supplies an exact represented relation [Dκ,X]=I+κs for every parameter; its proof uses the monomial action rather than an unsupported universal classification. These are constructive examples of obstruction, flatness with changing derived invariants, and a genuinely defined deformation law.

Poisson wall transport adds a geometric version. A skew lattice pairing gives an automorphism x^m↦x^m f(x^γ)^{B(γ,m)}. Skew symmetry and B(γ,γ)=0 ensure the distinguished monomial is fixed and make the inverse and bracket compatibility work. Replacing the pairing by an arbitrary matrix loses the proof. The same principle links back to Moyal exactness: each higher equation must actually vanish, and its degree or filtration bound determines whether a finite check is complete. The atlas presents finite obstruction calculations with exact coefficient rings and reports the boundary between formal existence, finite truncation, convergence and physical interpretation.

theorem_statement: Over a characteristic-two field, the C₂-character tangent u=1+ε modulo ε² satisfies u²=1 but cannot lift to u=1+η+bη² modulo η³. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from two, A_t=k[x]/(x²−t) has HH^n=0 for t≠0 and n>0, while at t=0 every positive-degree HH^n has dimension one.
theorem_proof: In characteristic two, (1+ε)²=1 because 2ε=ε²=0. For a prospective lift, (1+η+bη²)²=1+η² modulo η³: doubled terms vanish and the η² coefficient cannot be changed by b. Thus the tangent relation has an unavoidable next-order obstruction. For the flat algebra family, division by the monic polynomial leaves a unique representative a+bx, proving freeness of rank two. At t≠0, choose a²=t; x−a and x+a are coprime, so Chinese remainders give A_t≅k×k, a separable algebra with no positive-degree Hochschild cohomology. At t=0 the standard two-periodic bimodule resolution has maps x⊗1−1⊗x and x⊗1+1⊗x. Applying Hom over A^e gives alternating maps zero and multiplication by 2x. In positive degrees the kernels or cokernels have dimension one: ker(2x)=kx and A/(2x)=k. Thus flatness of the underlying module does not force derived-invariant constancy.
